statement:
You're not going to understand everything right away. Please ask your questions on our class message board! When you ask questions, other students benefit when they read and participate in the conversation. Instructors can also teach better when you ask questions, since it shows your thought process.

Below is the AoPS advice on how to ask a good question:

Most often, we ask others questions to get answers. But at AoPS, we won't just tell you what the next step is or what you need to do in order to get a perfect score. Instead, we'll help you understand the material and ask questions that help you develop your own critical thinking skills. This will allow you to solve the problem on your own.

Some students may find this frustrating because the homework is due that day, and they just want to be told what to do. Please understand that you will not learn as much this way, and we will not just give you the answer or solution.

**Moderate Level Question-Asking: Be Specific**

Statements like "Please help" or "I'm stuck" are very hard to answer. After all, there aren't any details there! These statements will generally get a response of "What do you need help with?" or "What are you stuck on?" or "What don't you understand?"

In order to get help, think carefully about what you're are stuck on and try to tell us about it in your question. Some examples are: "I don't understand what the question means when it says ____." "Can someone explain how (some property) applies to this problem?"

**Expert Level Question-Asking: Providing Background**

In addition to asking specific questions, great questions include some background. If we know about what you have already tried or how you're thinking about the problem, it will help us give better, more relevant tips. Expert-level questions look like this:

"I tried (some approach), but now I'm stuck. Can someone give me a hint?" "It seems like we can use (some property) on this problem. I can tell how it applies ____ but I'm stuck on how it works with ____. Any tips?"

Knowing what you are having trouble with is an important skill to develop. To help us assist you in the best way, try to figure out specifically what is stopping you from moving forward. Try to make your question as specific as possible. We are here to help you, but we need some information to directly respond to your inquiry.

**Getting Started**

Regarding homework questions, AoPS has a general policy that students should get the discussion started. If you tell us you have no idea how to start, we will prompt you to come up with an idea to get the ball rolling. It doesn't even have to be a good idea, but looking at a problem and coming up with ideas is an important problem-solving skill that we want you to practice. After you get in the habit of coming up with ideas, then you can sort out the good ones. __source__

Select the **three** statements that agree with the handbook's viewpoint on asking questions, as applied to a physics class.

Whoever answers the question should tell you the answer to the problem you're trying to solve.

Asking questions can be part of the process of solving a problem.

'"How do I get started on this problem?" is an expert level question

Questions should communicate what specific part of a problem you are stuck on.

It's often helpful to start your question about a problem by saying what laws of physics you think are relevant.

If you're stuck, it's the instructor's responsibility to tell you the first step on a problem to get you going.

statement:
On hot days you can sometimes see __mirages__.

PhysicsStuff.com

The reflection of people walking can make it look like there's a puddle of water on the ground, but there isn't.

A mirage happens when the air just above the ground is much warmer than the air higher up.

PhysicsStuff.com

Under these conditions, light will bend down and then up again, creating the mirage.

Madhav University

The diagram suggests there is a layer of hot air, then a layer of cold air, as if these layers were cleanly separated from each other. In fact, there's a gradient, with the temperature getting continuously cooler the further we go from the ground. A better diagram would show many different layers, or a gradient of color from red to blue indicating temperature.

Remember from class that light takes the path of least time between its starting and end points.

What does this imply about the speed of light through air?

Choose one.

The speed of light is always equal to $$c$$ by definition, so it doesn't imply anything.

The speed of light is faster in hot air than in cold air.

The speed of light is faster in cold air than in hot air.

The speed of light is slower in air than in a vacuum, but the same regardless of the air temperature.

Nothing; the light is pulled down by gravity, not the temperature of the air.

name: We will use __normalized scientific notation__ for both large and small numbers. In this…
desc: We will use __normalized scientific notation__ for both large and small numbers. In this notation, any number can be represented by a number (called the "coefficient") greater than $$1.0$$ and less than $$10,$$ multiplied by ten to some power. For example, here are some numbers…
statement:
We will use __normalized scientific notation__ for both large and small numbers. In this notation, any number can be represented by a number (called the "coefficient") greater than $$1.0$$ and less than $$10,$$ multiplied by ten to some power. For example, here are some numbers written in both the ordinary decimal notation and in normalized scientific notation.

The word "normalized" in "normalized scientific notation" means that the coefficient is greater than or equal to $$1$$ and less than $$10.$$ For example, $$42.1 \times 10^5$$ is in scientific notation, but not normalized scientific notation. In normalized scientific notation, we'd write $$4.21 \times 10^6$$ instead.

$$\begin{tabular}{ r | r } \text{decimal notation} & \text{normalized scientific notation} \\ \hline 350 & $$3.50 \times 10^2\,\,\;$$ \\ 10{,}005 & $$1.0005 \times 10^4\,\,\;$$ \\ 14.3 & $$1.43 \times 10^1\,\,\;$$ \\ 578{,}240.92 & $$5.7824092 \times 10^5\,\,\;$$\\ 0.00037 & $$3.7 \times 10^{-4}$$ \end{tabular}$$

If you would like a tutorial on scientific notation, there is one available on the class homepage.

We also want to report the results of our calculations to an appropriate number of __significant figures__.

For example, if a problem says that something travels $$2.2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$0.91 \;\mathrm{s},$$ it's reasonable to give the object's speed as $$2.4 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ but the precise calculation giving $$\dfrac{2.2 \;\mathrm{m}}{0.91 \;\mathrm{s}} = 2.417582\ldots \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ has digits that aren't meaningful, since the original measurements are not known to that level of detail.

In a lab report or scientific document, adding the extra digits could confuse the reader by making them think your data was far more precise than it really was. As a guideline, give your calculations to the same number of digits as used in the data.

--------------------

The speed of sound is usually faster in solids than in air. It's especially fast in beryllium, a rare metal that is exceptionally stiff and light. Beryllium is sometimes used when weight is extremely important, for example in satellites. A sample of beryllium looks like this:

By Alchemist-hp = Alchemist-hp (pse-mendelejew.de) - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=4283181

Suppose a student wants to find the speed of sound $$v$$ through a sample of beryllium. Using a micrometer (a device for precise distance measurements) and electronic timing equipment, they measure that sound travels $$1.08 \times 10^{-1} \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$8.51 \times 10^{-6} \;\mathrm{s}.$$ What speed of sound do they compute?

Give your answer in normalized scientific notation and to an appropriate number of significant figures.

statement:
In this problem, you'll practice __estimation__ and __unit conversions__. These are both essential skills that we'll use throughout the course.

--------

Estimate the average speed at which human hair grows in miles per hour.

There is no one answer to this question - different hairs grow at different rates, and grow unsteadily. Still, there is a range which is approximately correct. To be marked correct on this question you should be within one An __order of magnitude__ is a factor of ten, so your answer can be ten times as fast as ours, or ten times as slow, or anywhere between those limits. of our estimate.

In physics, when we estimate, we don't just guess our final answer. Instead, we start with something we know and work from there. Try to estimate the speed that hair grows based on some life experience you have, and use whatever units are most convenient. Then convert your units to miles per hour.

Here are a few conversion factors that could help:

$$\begin{aligned} 2.54 \;\mathrm{cm} & = 1 \;\mathrm{in} \\ 12 \;\mathrm{in} & = 1 \;\mathrm{ft} \\ 5280 \;\mathrm{ft} & = 1 \;\mathrm{mi} \\ \end{aligned}$$

You may also want to use conversion factors related to hours, days, months, or years.

Enter your answer using normalized scientific notation, meaning that the coefficient should be greater than or equal to one and less than ten.

statement:
In this problem, you'll practice the notation and interpretation of speed and velocity.

-------------------------

Below is a sketch of an __Atwood machine__, an 18th century invention intended to measure the strength of gravity. The device consists of a pulley (a circular ring that can easily spin, but otherwise can't move around left/right or up/down), a rope that goes over the pulley, and weights on either side of the rope. The box $$H$$ is heavier than the box $$L.$$

The weights are initially held with $$L$$ down low and $$H$$ up high, then released. $$H$$ will start falling downward, and it will pull on the rope as it falls, which pulls $$L$$ upward.

To help you visualize this motion, look at this gif:

"Low Friction Atwood Machine", mittechtv, YouTube

(In this gif one of the weights has some slight side-to-side wobble, which you should ignore. Model the motion as purely in the up/down direction.)

Let the velocity of the heavier box be $$v_{y;H}$$ and the lighter box $$v_{y;L}.$$ The speeds are $$v_H$$ and $$v_L.$$ We define the upward direction to be positive, so upward motion is a positive velocity.

One second after the boxes are released, we measure the velocities $$v_{y;H}$$ and $$v_{y;L}.$$ (The boxes don't hit the ground or reach the pulley in this one second.)

Which statements below are true? Select two.

You do not need to find the values of $$v_{y;H}$$ or $$v_{y;L},$$ or make any quantitative measurements, to answer this question.

Note that statements (a) and (b) are about velocities. (c) through (e) are about speeds.

$$v_{y;L} = - v_{y;H}$$

$$v_{y;L} = v_{y;H}$$

$$v_H > v_L$$

$$v_H < v_L$$

$$v_H = v_L$$

Ayesha McGowan is a professional road racing cyclist.

Jeff Clark, https://www.liv-cycling.com/global/campaigns/representation-matters-ayesha-mcgowan/23833

In 2021, McGowan competed in a multi-day race near Avignon, France. The race took her into the western portion of the Alps mountain range. As you would expect, she rode relatively slowly when climbing steep mountains and very fast when coming down.

McGowan's bike has a computer that records its speed. After her rides, McGowan shares data on her speed versus time, along with some other data, publicly on the internet. Below is a plot of some of Ayesha's data during one day of the race. Time is indicated along the top. The total time was close to four hours.

How far did McGowan ride this day?

Your answer should be accurate to within $$20 \;\mathrm{mi}.$$

We haven't worked on a problem like this yet, but you can still do it! Start by finding McGowan's average speed as closely as you can based on the graph.

Take a look at the following dot diagram. The dots were made $$1 \;\mathrm{s}$$ apart, and the scale is $$1:1,$$ so the dots' distance apart on your computer monitor is their distance apart in real life.

The dots should display the correct distance apart on most computers. However, if your browser is not set to a $$100\%$$ zoom, or for various other reasons, it's possible the dots will not display correctly for you. The distance between the last two dots should be about $$3.9 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$ If it is not, you can multiply all your distances by a scaling factor to answer this question. For example, if you measure that distance to be $$3.0 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ you can multiply all your measurements by $$\dfrac{3.9 \;\mathrm{cm}}{3.0 \;\mathrm{cm}} = 1.3$$

**a)**

Did the object modeled by this dot diagram have positive or negative velocity? How do you know? If it's impossible to tell, explain why.

statement:
In August 2022, a woman in Vancouver rented a car for three days. When she returned it, the rental company billed her more than $$\$9{,}000.$$ The company said its rate was $$\dfrac{\$0.25}{\mathrm{km}}$$ and that she had driven $$36{,}482\;\mathrm{km}$$ during the rental.

Show that this bill cannot describe a real trip by finding the average speed the car would need to cover $$36{,}482\;\mathrm{km}$$ in three days, and converting that speed into everyday units. What most likely happened?

Useful facts: there are $$24\;\mathrm{h}$$ in a day, $$5\;\mathrm{km}\approx 3\;\mathrm{mi},$$ and Earth's circumference is about $$40{,}000\;\mathrm{km}.$$

desc: You want to measure a cyclist's speed from a video. The video plays at $$20$$ frames per second. By comparing the bicycle to a known length — its __wheelbase__ of $$0.977\;\mathrm{m}$$ — you can turn pixel measurements in the video into real distances. In the video, the…
statement:
You want to measure a cyclist's speed from a video. The video plays at $$20$$ frames per second. By comparing the bicycle to a known length — its __wheelbase__ of $$0.977\;\mathrm{m}$$ — you can turn pixel measurements in the video into real distances.

In the video, the wheelbase measures $$65$$ pixels. Between frame $$18$$ and frame $$20,$$ the bicycle's front wheel advances $$47$$ pixels along the road.

__(a)__ How far, in meters, did the bicycle move between frame 18 and frame 20?

__(b)__ How much time elapsed between those two frames?

__(c)__ What was the cyclist's average speed over this interval?

__(d)__ Suppose the $$47$$-pixel measurement could be off by as much as $$2$$ pixels. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the distance, and write the speed in the form (value) $$\pm$$ (uncertainty).

statement:
A skater rides back and forth on a curved ramp. We describe her location with a coordinate $$x$$ measured __along the track__ from the left edge. The simulation marks the track with evenly spaced dashes — $$4$$ dashes per meter — numbered starting from the left edge.

__(a)__ In the picture above, the skater is at dash $$10.$$ What is her coordinate $$x$$ (her distance from the left edge, measured along the track)?

__(b)__ Explain the difference between the skater's __position__ and her __coordinate__.

__(c)__ Now suppose we move the origin so that $$x=0$$ is at the lowest point of the ramp instead of the left edge, giving a new coordinate $$x'$$ (shown below). For each of the following, state whether it changes: her position, her coordinate, her speed, and her displacement between two instants.

__(d)__ Her average velocity between two instants is $$v_x=\dfrac{x_2-x_1}{t_2-t_1}=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}.$$ If she is moving to the left (toward smaller $$x$$), what is the sign of $$v_x$$? How are her speed $$v$$ and her velocity $$v_x$$ related?

label: MCH01
name: The Speed of Light — In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly spinning toothed…
desc: In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly spinning toothed wheel (a __cog__) and a distant mirror. Light passes through a gap between two teeth, travels to a mirror $$8.0\;\mathrm{km}$$ away, and reflects straight back toward the wheel. If the wheel…
statement:
In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly spinning toothed wheel (a __cog__) and a distant mirror. Light passes through a gap between two teeth, travels to a mirror $$8.0\;\mathrm{km}$$ away, and reflects straight back toward the wheel.

If the wheel turns slowly, the light returns through the same gap and is seen. Fizeau sped the wheel up until, at $$13.7$$ revolutions per second, the returning light was just blocked: while the light made its round trip, the wheel turned just far enough for the next __tooth__ to move into the gap's place.

The wheel has $$720$$ teeth (and $$720$$ gaps between them). Find Fizeau's value for the speed of light, $$c.$$

Hint: with $$720$$ teeth and $$720$$ gaps there are $$1440$$ equal segments around the wheel. Being blocked by the next tooth means the wheel rotated by exactly one of these segments during the light's round trip.

label: MCH01
name: Bending Light — Light travels more slowly through glass than through empty space. In a typical glass it…
desc: Light travels more slowly through glass than through empty space. In a typical glass it moves at about $$0.7c,$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light in vacuum (about $$3\times10^8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$). Consider a beam of light that goes from a point $$A$$ in vacuum to a point $$B$$…
statement:
Light travels more slowly through glass than through empty space. In a typical glass it moves at about $$0.7c,$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light in vacuum (about $$3\times10^8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$).

Consider a beam of light that goes from a point $$A$$ in vacuum to a point $$B$$ inside a glass block. It could follow many different paths; physicists model light as taking the __path of least time__. The figure below shows $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and two possible paths: a straight dashed path and a bent solid path.

__(a)__ The straight-line path from $$A$$ to $$B$$ is the shortest in distance. Give a reason it might __not__ be the path of least time.

__(b)__ Use __extreme cases__ to build intuition: predict the kind of path light takes (i) if the glass slowed light a billion-fold, and (ii) if the glass slowed light by only a tiny amount (say $$0.00001\%$$).

__(c)__ Using the least-time idea, explain why light __bends__ (refracts) as it crosses from vacuum into glass.

__(d)__ A lens is a piece of glass shaped so that __every__ path from $$A$$ to $$B$$ takes the same amount of time, as in the figure below. Explain what this does to the light.

label: MCH01
name: Distant Galaxies — Astronomers find that essentially every distant galaxy is moving __away__ from us, and…
desc: Astronomers find that essentially every distant galaxy is moving __away__ from us, and that a galaxy's recession speed $$v$$ is proportional to its distance $$D$$ from us: $$v=H_0\,D,$$ where $$H_0$$ is a constant (the __Hubble constant__). The graph below shows this pattern —…
statement:
Astronomers find that essentially every distant galaxy is moving __away__ from us, and that a galaxy's recession speed $$v$$ is proportional to its distance $$D$$ from us: $$v=H_0\,D,$$ where $$H_0$$ is a constant (the __Hubble constant__). The graph below shows this pattern — each point is a galaxy, and galaxies that are farther away recede faster.

To interpret this law, work a toy model with simple numbers. Take $$H_0=0.5\;\dfrac{\mathrm{m/s}}{\mathrm{m}}$$ (half a meter per second, per meter), and assume each object has always moved at a constant speed.

__(a)__ An object is $$D=3\;\mathrm{m}$$ away. Find its speed $$v,$$ and how long ago it was at our location.

__(b)__ Repeat for an object $$D=4\;\mathrm{m}$$ away.

__(c)__ Now take a general distance $$D.$$ Show that the time since the object was at our location is the same for __every__ object, and express that time using $$H_0.$$

__(d)__ What is the physical meaning of $$\dfrac{1}{H_0},$$ and what surprising conclusion does this simple model suggest about the past of the universe?

statement:
This problem asks you to think qualitatively about acceleration and free fall. You'll visualize acceleration using a free falling stick.

-------------------------------

There is a challenge that many people find surprising: hold a dollar bill vertically and invite a friend to put two fingers on either side of it, near the bottom, ready to grab the dollar bill.

Chegg, https://www.chegg.com/homework-help/questions-and-answers/classic-trick-person-1-hangs-dollar-bill-hand-dangles-fingers-person-2-person-1-releases-b-q31489919

Ask your friend to try to catch the dollar after you drop it, but without moving their hand down. (This is pretty fun - try it yourself with a friend of family member!)

Free fall acceleration is high enough that almost no one can react quickly enough to catch the dollar.

Suppose you want to modify this idea to measure your friend's reaction time. Instead of dropping a dollar, you'll drop a stick that's long enough that your friend will be able to catch it.

You know $$g,$$ the local free fall acceleration, so you can calculate how the stick will fall. You put marks on the stick labeled with times in such a way that when your friend grabs it, their fingers are at a mark corresponding to their reaction time.

For example, if your friend's reaction time is $$0.25 \;\mathrm{s},$$ then when they catch the stick, their fingers will be on top of a mark on the stick labeled $$``0.25 \;\mathrm{s}".$$ Your markings will correspond to reaction times of $$0.05 \;\mathrm{s}, 0.10 \;\mathrm{s}, 0.15 \;\mathrm{s}$$ etc. starting at the bottom of the stick and increasing up to the top.

Which of the following shows the correct spacing between the marks on the stick?

statement:
On their wedding day, a couple jumped off a cliff into water below. (As a celebration, not out of despair.)

Zvonimir Barisin

There's another photo taken just before they hit the water. In this question, we'll try to figure out what that photo looks like. (That photo is included in the solution.) This gives us more qualitative practice with free fall acceleration.

-----------------------------------

To model the jump of bride and groom off a cliff, we make some simplifications: - assume they both are falling vertically from the same height, but the bride started falling a moment before the groom - ignore air drag - ignore that they are holding hands - model each person as a point at their __center of mass__. This is intuively the center spot of a person. When standing, it's roughly few inches behind the belly button

Then we can define a few terms related to the gap between bride and groom:

__separation:__ how far beneath the groom the bride is __speed gap__: the difference in speed between the bride and groom __acceleration gap__: the difference in magnitude of acceleration between the bride and groom __time gap__: the time between the bride reaching a certain height and the groom reaching that same height

As the couple fell and before they hit the water, these quantities may have changed. **Categorize each according to whether it increased, stayed the same, or decreased.** Categories can hold multiple quantities, and categories are allowed to be empty. Every quantity needs to go in one category.

Reflecting on your answers, try to guess what the photo taken just before they hit the water looks like.

The difficulty of the problem set is starting to increase around here, so expect to think longer and make some false starts on the later problems. The harder you work on a problem, the better it feels to finally solve it. Remember that after you've given a problem some thought, the message boards are there for discussion.

--------

A car is moving at velocity $$v_{x0}$$ along the positive $$x$$ direction. The driver needs to stop suddenly.

Then: 1) The car will continue at its original velocity $$v_{x0}$$ for a short time $$t_r$$ until the driver hits the brakes. $$t_r$$ is the driver's reaction time. 2) The car will get slower and slower as the driver presses the brakes. The acceleration is $$a_x.$$ Eventually the car stops.

During the second phase, constant acceleration is a fairly good model for most cars.

Note that $$v_{x0} >0$$ and $$a_x < 0$$ due to the directions of motion and acceleration.

Below is a plot of $$v_x,$$ over time in this model, beginning at the moment the driver sees a problem and ending shortly after the car stops.

Find the distance $$\Delta x$$ the car moves before stopping in terms of $$v_{x0}, t_r,$$ and $$a_x.$$

Part B. Young people generally have somewhat faster reaction times than elderly people.

Suppose that an elderly driver drives at $$v_{x0; \mathrm{elderly}} = 25 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (about $$56 \;\mathrm{mph})$$ and the distance they need to come to a complete stop is $$\Delta x = 60 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

A cocky young driver thinks their faster reaction time allows them to drive safely at a higher speed. Assume the reaction times are $$t_{r;\mathrm{elderly}} = 0.6 \;\mathrm{s}$$ for the elderly driver and $$t_{r;\mathrm{young}} = 0.4 \;\mathrm{s}$$ for the young driver, and that $$a_x$$ is the same for each driver.

The young driver needs to stop in the same distance, $$\Delta x = 60 \;\mathrm{m},$$ as the elderly driver. What is the maximum possible initial speed $$v_{x0;\mathrm{young}}$$ for the young driver such that they can still stop within a distance $$\Delta x?$$

Use the model you developed in the previous question to answer this one. Your answer should be accurate to within $$0.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

This is one of the later problems on the set, and it's a multi-step problem that is probably going to take you little time, plus at least a sheet full of scratch work. It's okay to make false starts on problems like these, and a great idea to discuss them in the homework forum after you've worked on them a bit. Our homeworks will generally start with short problems you might be able to do in one step and build towards more complex problems like this one.

You won't be able to take a couple of numbers from the problem, put them in a single equation, and get the answer. Instead, first work on making a __plan__ for how you'll solve the problem. For example, ask yourself whether there is some quantity you could calculate which isn't the answer, but would be helpful in finding the answer.

The acceleration $$a_x$$ is something like that, so you could break the problem down into: 1) Use the given information to find $$a_x$$ 2) Use $$a_x$$ to figure out $$v_{x0;\mathrm{young}}$$ You may need to break those steps down further as well to figure out how you're going to find $$a_x$$ and what you're going to do with it once you have it.

statement:
Part A. In this multi-part problem, you'll practice several stages of conducting an experiment, including understanding what the experiment is for, building a model of what happens in the experiment, deciding what data to collect, deciding how to analyze that data, and drawing conclusions from the experiment.

-----------------------------------

An __Atwood machine__ is a rope with weights on either end. The rope hangs over a pulley. The weights usually have different mass, and the more massive weight accelerates towards the ground while the less massive weight accelerates upward.

"Low Friction Atwood Machine", mittechtv, YouTube

You can assume the weights move with constant acceleration and that they are released from rest.

We can use an Atwood machine to measure $$g,$$ assuming we have a model of the acceleration of the machine that includes $$g.$$ Later, we will build such a model, but we'll ignore complications like the weight of the string or friction in the pulley.

A different experiment to measure $$g$$ is simply to drop an object and time how long it takes to fall. There are several differences between this free fall experiment and an experiment using the Atwood machine.

Most of these differences make the Atwood experiment more accurate than the free fall experiment, but one does not. **Select the one difference that makes the Atwood machine __less__ accurate than a similar free fall experiment.**

You can assume that in both experiments, the times are being taken by a single person with a stopwatch.

There is friction in the pulley of the Atwood machine, but negligible friction in free fall (because air drag is very small). Assume our models do not account for friction.

The Atwood machine has a much lower acceleration than free fall.

We can take data with many different sets of weights in the Atwood machine. This gives different accelerations. In free fall, all weights have the same acceleration.

In the Atwood machine, we can release the lighter weight from ground level and find the time for the heavier weight to reach the ground. This makes the starting and ending points we're timing right next to each other, rather than far apart as for free fall.

Part B. Before we try an experiment with the Atwood machine, we should understand how we expect it to behave. A good way to start building our intuition for it is to think about extreme cases, or special cases. These are special values of the weights such that the behavior of the Atwood machine is easier to understand.

There are two extreme / special cases we should check: equal masses and very uneven masses.

We can call the mass of the heavier box $$m_H$$ and the mass of the lighter box $$m_L.$$ Then the equal masses special case is $$m_H = m_L.$$ The very uneven masses extreme case is $$m_H \gg m_L.$$ You can imagine that the heavier box has the mass of an entire mountain (but somehow still fits in the same size box) and the lighter box has the mass of a single flea.

What should the magnitude of acceleration of the Atwood machine be in each case?

Part C. Now we'll try to select a model for the acceleration of the Atwood machine.

In the Atwood machine, if we double $$m_H$$ and also double $$m_L,$$ it's as if we simply had two copies of the Atwood machine right next to each other, with the masses lightly touching. The two copies would each run with the same acceleration as each other, so doubling each mass in this way doesn't affect the acceleration.

Extending this argument, it's only the ratio of masses, $$\dfrac{m_L}{m_H},$$ that affects the acceleration. We can call this ratio $$r.$$

$$r$$ is always between zero and one, since by definition the denominator is bigger than the numerator.

Part F. In this optional discussion problem, you conduct the experiment at home, share your results, and discuss your and other experiments with your classmates.

---------

If you would like to do some hands on experimentation, build your own Atwood machine at home. You are welcome to buy a pulley, but you could also run some string over any smooth rod with low friction. If you can wrap a portion of a broom handle in Teflon tape, that may make a low-friction surface to support your rope. You could also try making your own pulley using instructions you find online.

A stack of coins makes a convenient way to adjust the masses in your Atwood machine.

If you collect data, find accelerations, plot them, and find $$g,$$ share how you made your Atwood machine and your plot to the class forum. You can also see what other students did and compare results and techniques.

If you are having trouble finding suitable materials, you could also take data using a simulated Atwood machine, such as this one: (http://physics.bu.edu/~duffy/HTML5/Atwoods_machine.html)

Part B. This part of the problem lets you practice algebra skills in physical modeling.

-------------------------------

Because the horizontal component of velocity is constant in projectile motion, an equation for the horizontal position over time of some small piece of water shot out of the fountain is $$x = x_0 + v_{x0}t.$$

And an equation for the vertical position over time is $$y = y_0 + v_{y0} t - \dfrac12 g t^2.$$

The initial positions $$x_0$$ and $$y_0$$ only depend on our choice of origin, so they don't model any useful information about the speed of the water. We can also choose the time $$t = 0$$ to be when the water is moving horizontally, so $$v_{y0} = 0.$$ That lets us simplify to $$\begin{aligned}x & = v_{x0} t \\ y & = y_0 - \dfrac12 g t^2 \end{aligned}$$

Find $$y$$ as a function of $$x.$$

Then, assuming $$g = 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and using your answer from part (A), find $$v_{x0},$$ the horizontal speed of the water.

You should be accurate to within $$1 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Give your answer to the nearest $$ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

statement:
This problem is for practice with two different skills. First, there's a lot of interpreting the meaning of different mathematical notation. Second, there's understanding what scientific hypothesis mean, and when two differently stated hypotheses are actually the same thing.

--------

In class, we generated the hypothesis that the quantity $$v^2 + 2gy$$ is conserved along an object's trajectory when we use a model that: - the object can be modeled as a single point - there is free fall acceleration - there can be other simple influences, such as sliding or swinging on a string, known as "constraints" - friction, air drag, and similar complications are negligible

Now let's imagine several other physics classes, each of which came up with their own hypothesis for the same type of motion. Each answer choice to this question is one of the hypotheses.

Most of these hypotheses may make the same prediction as ours in every circumstance. In that case, the two hypothesis is equivalent to ours. We could say they are the same hypothesis written in different mathematical notation. Experiments cannot give evidence favoring any one of the various equivalent hypotheses.

Two of hypotheses below are different. They each make different predictions than ours (and than each other). Experiments can favor one hypothesis in particular between those two hypotheses and ours.

__Select the **two** hypotheses that are **not** equivalent to our hypothesis.__

The variables in these hypotheses have the same definitions as our variables, with the addition that $$h$$ is a height (a specific value that $$y$$ could take) that is constant throughout any given experiment, but can be different from experiment to experiment. Also, $$\Delta$$ is used to mean "change in", so $$\Delta (v^2)$$ is how much the quantity $$v^2$$ has changed since the beginning of the experiment.

When there is a hypothesis stated as an equation, the hypothesis is that the equation is true at all times during the experiment.

Our hypothesis: $$v^2 + 2gy$$ is conserved.

$$\dfrac12v^2 + gy$$ is conserved

$$v + \sqrt{2gy}$$ is conserved

$$v^2 + 2g(y-h)$$ is conserved

$$\dfrac12 m v^2 = - mg (y - h)$$

$$v^2 = -2gy$$

$$\Delta (v^2) = - \Delta (2gy)$$

name: When a ball bounces off the ground, it loses some kinetic energy, so if the vertical…
desc: When a ball bounces off the ground, it loses some kinetic energy, so if the vertical component of the ball's velocity is $$v_{y0}$$ just before hitting the ground and $$v_{yb}$$ just after bouncing, then $$v_{yb} < -v_{y0}.$$ $$v_y$$ is positive in the upward direction, so…
statement:
When a ball bounces off the ground, it loses some kinetic energy, so if the vertical component of the ball's velocity is $$v_{y0}$$ just before hitting the ground and $$v_{yb}$$ just after bouncing, then $$v_{yb} < -v_{y0}.$$

$$v_y$$ is positive in the upward direction, so $$v_{y0} < 0,$$ since the ball is moving down just before bouncing. The inequality $$v_{yb} < -v_{y0}$$ is comparing two positive quantities, and is saying the same thing as $$|v_{yb}| < |v_{y0}|\,.$$

One simple model says that when a ball bounces, there is always the same ratio between $$v_{y0}$$ and $$v_{yb}\,.$$

For example, suppose a ball bounces off a floor with $$v_{y0} = -4 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and then bounces with $$v_{yb} = 3 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ This model would say that $$v_{yb} = -\dfrac34 v_{y0}$$ for any bounce. If the ball were instead approaching the floor with $$v_{y0} = -6 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ the model says that $$v_{yb}$$ would be $$v_{yb} = -\dfrac34 \cdot 6 \;\mathrm{m/s} = 4.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

The ratio of $$v_{yb}$$ to $$-v_{y0}$$ is called the __coefficient of restitution__, and often given the symbol $$e.$$ We can write this as the equation $$e = \dfrac{-v_{yb}}{v_{y0}}.$$

Although the bowling ball is quickly approaching the physicist's face, the physicist doesn't flinch; they are confident that, due to conservation of energy, the ball cannot rise higher than it was released from and will turn around before making contact.

This demo is dangerous - the bowling ball sometimes hits the physicist and can injure them!

statement:
Part A. This multi-part problem explores an important physics technology - a particle collider. It lets you practice with energy conceptually without worrying about the details of calculations. However, it introduces lots of new context, and requires careful interpretation of the graphs and figures.

---------------------------

The main way that physicists study the structure of subatomic particles is with __particle accelerators__. These are giant machines (kilometers long) that accelerate particles to very high speed before crashing them into each other. By studying the debris, physicists can learn more about particles and their interactions.

Below is a diagram illustrating a __linear__ accelerator. (Other accelerators make particles go in a circle.)

By Chetvorno - Own work, CC0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=68477306

The cylinders labelled $$C_1, C_2,$$ etc. are called __klystrons__.

The red dots are particles. The green line shows the potential energy of the particles as a function of distance down the line. (The simulation uses $$V$$ instead of $$U$$ for potential energy.)

The setup has to be timed precisely so that the time it takes a particle to cross a klystron is the same as the time for the green line to flip upside down.

(The potential energy in this case is electrical potential energy, but we don't need to be concerned with where the potential energy comes from for this question.)

Why do the klystrons get longer as we move towards the right?

the potential energy of the particle is increasing, so klystrons have to be longer to contain it

the particle is accelerating, so it travels further in the time it takes the green line to flip upside down

the particle velocity constantly switches from positive to negative, so the klystrons alternate in size

Part C. Particle physicists often measure the energy of particles in __electron-volts,__ $$\mathrm{eV}.$$

Electron-volts are related to joules by

$$1 \;\mathrm{eV} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \;\mathrm{J}$$

The mass of an electron is $$ m_e \approx 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

Old TVs and computer monitors used simple particle accelerators called __cathode ray tubes__, which accelerated electrons from the back of the device to the screen in front. When electrons hit the screen, they made it light up in that particular spot. TVs and computer monitors did this many times per second all over the screen to make images.

A cathode ray tube inside an early Macintosh Computer By © Cody Logan / Wikimedia Commons / "Macintosh Plus interior", CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=71940343

Electrons gained a kinetic energy of around $$KE = 3 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{eV}$$ while shooting from the back of the TV to the screen.

Part A. Over this multi-part problem, we'll engage with a real scientific research project that used the physics concepts we've recently been studying.

------------------

The fastest animal in the world is the peregrine falcon. It hunts by flying high in the sky until it sees a small bird below it. Then the peregrine dives at the small bird from above. Peregrines reach up to $$108 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (242 mph) while diving.

National Geograph, "Skydiving Falcon", YouTube

In 2014, a team of German scientists trained peregrine falcons to dive in front of a dam and recorded the dives with high-resolution video.

Ponitz, Benjamin, et al. "Diving-flight aerodynamics of a peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus)." PLoS One 9.2 (2014): e86506.

You can assume the falcons began their dive from the top of the dam. They do not "fly downward"; they are in a tucked position and are pulled down by gravity while diving.

Based on the photos of the dam, did the falcons in the study reach speeds above $$100 \;\mathrm{m/s}?$$

Yes; that's the speed peregrine falcons dive, so that's how fast they went in this study

No; the dam is too short to allow that

The peregrine is initially in free fall, but as it falls faster and faster, it encounters more and more air drag. Eventually, the peregrine falls at some maximum speed, given its size, shape, and the air it's falling through. This maximum speed is the falcon's __terminal velocity__.

Match each plot to whether it shows the height, speed, or magnitude of acceleration of a peregrine falling through air, starting from rest, as a function of time. These plots only show the portion of the dive while the peregrin is approaching terminal velocity. They do not show the bird pulling out of the dive, capturing prey, landing on the ground, etc.

Part C. Draw a plot of the kinetic, thermal, gravitational potential, and total energies as a peregrine falcon dives, starting from rest and reaching terminal velocity. Start your plots right when the falcon starts diving. Stop the plots before the falcon pulls out of its dive.

Your drawing should show four curves, one for each energy you're plotting. The curves should all be plotted on the same set of axes. Label the curves according to which type of energy they represent. You should also label the axes, but you don't need a scale for them.

The roiling air behind the falcon technically has kinetic energy, but in a matter of seconds, that kinetic energy will be dissipated to thermal energy, so you can count any energy in the air as thermal energy in this problem. For thermal energy, draw the change in thermal energy from the time that the falcon starts diving, so this curve should begin at zero.

Your plot can be qualitative, but should show the trend in each type of energy.

For this part, you can turn in a labelled plot without detailed written explanation.

Part D. In class, we built a model for air drag. In this model, an object moving through the air leaves a tube of roiling air behind it. The speed of the air is similar to the object's own speed, and the tube's cross-sectional area is similar to the object's own cross-sectional area.

In their research, the German scientists found that the cross-sectional area of a typical diving peregrine was about $$0.012 \;\mathrm{m}^2.$$ The density of air is about $$1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ These quantities are approximations, but they are accurate to within $$10\%$$ or better for real peregrines diving close to $$90 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Note: all the measurements given in this problem are accurate enough to find a terminal velocity close to the observed terminal velocity of real peregrines, given the right model. If there is a discrepancy between your calculation and the real terminal velocity, look for it in the model, not in the figures you used.

statement:
A __Roberval balance__ is a device with six pivots as shown.

The bars cannot change length, and the device is rigid except at the pivots. The top and bottom horizontal bars are each single pieces, not two pieces coming together at the pivot.

The Roberval balance has only a single __degree of freedom__, or a single way of moving. After undergoing a displacement, it can look like either of these:

Or it can move larger or smaller amounts in the same way. The Roberval balance is in equilibrium at all these positions when no masses are added to it.

You can see the motion of the Roberval balance in the gif below:

A disc of mass $$m_L$$ is placed at the far left of the left hand bar, and a disc of mass $$m_R$$ is placed on the right hand bar near the vertical crossbar as shown.

Two students are discussing what the relationship should be between $$m_L$$ and $$m_R$$ for the device to be in equilibrium.

Duante says: The law of the lever says that the disc further from the fulcrum should have less mass, so for a lever, $$m_L < m_R.$$ We derived this by thinking about potential energy changes. The Roberval balance can be analyzed using energy, too, so $$m_L < m_R$$ is still correct.

Divya says: But here, there's no single fulcrum, like there is for a lever. We can't analyze this device using energy. We need to use virtual displacements instead. When the Roberval balance moves a little, the left and right discs each have the same virtual displacement, so $$m_L = m_R.$$

From the choices below, select one **incorrect** thing a student said.

Duante's final conclusion, $$m_L < m_R$$

Divya's final conclusion, $$m_L = m_R$$

Duante's claim that we can use potential energy to analyze the device

Divya's claim that we can use virtual displacements to analyze the device

Radio stations say things like "This is 101.5 FM." This means that the radio station's signal oscillates at frequency of $$101.5 \;\mathrm{MHz} = 1.015 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ To listen to this station, your radio needs to find any radio waves with that frequency and ignore all other radio waves around it.

The radio does this with a "tuner". A simple model for a tuner has two components: an __inductor__ and a __capacitor__. These are devices used in electric circuits. They both store energy. The inductor stores energy when electric charge runs through it, and the capacitor stores energy when there is electric charge on it.

Charge will oscillate between the inductor and capacitor at a certain frequency, which depends on how strong the inductor and capacitor are.

PhET project, "Circuit Construction Kit: DC", https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/circuit-construction-kit-dc

In this animation, the inductor is the coil of wire at the bottom. The capacitor is the two parallel plates at the top. The blue circles are charge. On the left, there is a white circle which can be ignored; in real life the circuit can work without it.

In radios, turning the tuning dial changes the capacitor, affecting the frequency of charge oscillations.

When the frequency of charge oscillations in the tuner is $$1.015 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ the radio waves from station 101.5 FM will have the same frequency as the tuner. Then the radio waves will push charge around in the tuner. The radio can detect the precise way that charge is moving and turn it into sound.

Other radio stations with different frequencies will not set a significant amount of charge oscillating in the tuner.

The energy stored by a capacitor can be modeled as $$E_C = \dfrac12 \dfrac{1}{C} Q^2$$ where $$Q$$ is the charge on the capacitor and $$C$$ is the __capacitance__, a measure of how large a capacitor it is. This is a potential energy.

The energy stored by an inductor can be modeled as $$ E_I = \dfrac12 L i^2$$ where $$L$$ is the __inductance__, a measure of how strong the inductor is, and $$i$$ is how fast charge runs through the inductor, so $$i$$ is similar to a speed, but for charge. You can think of $$i$$ as a rate of change of $$Q.$$ You can think of the energy in the inductor as playing a role similar to kinetic energy.

You change the tuner on a radio from 101.5 FM to 98.0 FM.

As you do, the capacitance $$C$$ of the capacitor gets multiplied by some factor. What is that factor?

Give your answer as a decimal to three decimal places.

Try making an analogy between the energy formulas for the circuit and the formulas for a mass on a spring. What quantity in a circuit can replace $$x,$$ the position of a mass on a spring? What circuit quantity can replace $$s,$$ the speed of the mass? (There is a hint to the answer to this question in the problem itself.) Once you know that, you should be able to find analogies for the spring constant and mass as well, then get a formula for the frequency of oscillations of the circuit based on the formula for the mass on a spring.

Part C. In this short video, there are two tuning forks. Each plays a note, and to many people, the notes sound like they have the same pitch. However, when the two tuning forks are hit simultaneously, there is a "wa-wa-wa" sound, called "beats".

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V8W4Djz6jnY

The "wa-wa-wa" sound occurs when two musicians are tuning, trying to play the same note, but actually playing at slightly different frequencies. It's the effect of the total sound from the two instruments getting louder, then softer, over and over. The beats disappear when the musicians are in tune.

The beats are similar to the phenomenon with pendulums of slightly different lengths. When the pendulums are totally out of sync (one to the left while the other is to the right), it's analogous to the soft part of the "wa-wa-wa" cycle. When the pendulums are in sync, it's analogous to the loud part. The pendulums had a period of about $$2.4 \;\mathrm{s},$$ but it took them about $$190 \;\mathrm{s}$$ to cycle from in sync to out of sync and back again.

Because beats are much slower than the frequencies that make them, they're easier to measure. They even apply to radio waves - the signals are much too fast to hear, but you can think of a radio tuner as measuring not just one frequency, but several very nearby ones that make beats in just such a way that it turns into music (or talking, if that's the type of radio you listen to)!

We wanted to include the video of beats so you could hear it before answering the next question. We can't include videos in a question that also has multiple choice buttons, so this "reading problem" holds the video and the next problem has a question about it.

desc: Part A. In week 5, we studied energy generated by wind turbines, and in the process we mentioned that fish leave trails of whirling patches of water behind them. The whirling patches of water are called __vortices__, and the phenomenon is called __vortex shedding__. (The entire…
statement:
Part A. In week 5, we studied energy generated by wind turbines, and in the process we mentioned that fish leave trails of whirling patches of water behind them. The whirling patches of water are called __vortices__, and the phenomenon is called __vortex shedding__. (The entire pattern of vortices behind the fish is also called its __von Kármán vortex street__.)

The same phenomenon can happen in many other situations. For example, the vortices form behind this tiger walking through algae-covered water https://www.reddit.com/r/woahdude/comments/7s4dw7/this_tiger_walking_through_algae/

They also form as wind blows around islands, like Guadalupe Island in the Pacific, off the shores of Mexico.

MODIS Rapid Response Project at NASA GSFC

The vortices form at a regular frequency. Here is an animation of the process:

By Cesareo de La Rosa Siqueira - http://www.mcef.ep.usp.br/staff/jmeneg/cesareo/vort2.gif, Attribution, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=87351

The theory of vortex shedding involves concepts from __fluid dynamics__, which would require an entire course to study. However, a model for vortex shedding says that whether we look at small examples like the fish or large examples like the island, $$L \approx 5D$$ where $$L$$ is the distance between two adjacent vortices that spin the same way, for example two purple vortices in the animation. $$D$$ is the diameter of the object that the vortices shed off of.

For Guadalupe Island, $$D \approx 8 \;\mathrm{km}$$ when the wind blows to the southeast, as in the photo. At the time of the photo, the wind was blowing about $$9 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at the island (and had been blowing at that speed for some time).

**What is the frequency of vortex shedding in the Guadalupe Island picture?**

The frequency is defined as the rate at which __pairs__ of vortices, one in each direction, shed off the island. This means the period is equal to the time between two successive clockwise-rotating vortices being created.

Note that the units are per hour, not hertz.

mathjax: $$ f = \blank \;\mathrm{hr}^{-1}$$

allowed: 1.023456789

Part B. Vortex shedding can be dangerous in objects that have a natural oscillation frequency of their own. If the frequency of vortex shedding matches the frequency of oscillations in the object, vortex shedding can cause very large and potentially-destructive oscillations.

For example, in the handout we saw that the wing of an airplane can oscillate:

If the airplane wing also begins vortex shedding at the same frequency as the wing's oscillations, each vortex can wind up pushing the wing to higher and higher amplitudes, eventually damaging or destroying it. This is extremely unlikely in modern airplanes because engineers are aware of the effect and design wings to avoid it, but it destroyed several airplanes in the past.

In 1940, the Washington Toll Bridge Authority constructed a large suspension bridge across the Tacoma Narrows Strait of Puget Sound, south of Seattle. Whenever the wind blew, the bridge would shake dramatically. Then on November 7, 1940, there were particularly strong winds of about $$18 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ that started violent oscillations of the bridge.

Barney Elliot, Stillman Fires Collection https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_destruction.ogv

This gif is in real time; it is not sped up or slowed down.

Eventually, the bridge collapsed.

Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=9002953

Engineers thought that perhaps the bridge was vortex-shedding at its own natural oscillation frequency, leading to bigger and bigger oscillations, then the collapse.

For the bridge, $$D$$ is the thickness of the roadway, as seen from the side, which was about $$D \approx 2.5 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

Is the vortex-shedding explanation plausible?

Yes, vortex shedding had about the same frequency as the oscillations that destroyed the bridge.

No, the bridge's oscillations had significantly __higher__ frequency than vortex shedding that day.

No, the bridge's oscillations had significantly __lower__ frequency than vortex shedding that day.

Part B. In Galileo's time, there were both __geocentric__ and __heliocentric__ models of the solar system. Geocentric models held that the Earth is at the center of the universe. Heliocentric models put the sun at the center. Although the modern understanding of astronomy doesn't match either model perfectly, you can think of the heliocentric model as essentially the same as the picture of the solar system you have learned. In part (A), you used the heliocentric model to make calculations.

Heliocentric and geocentric models made very similar predictions about the positions of planets in the sky. The existing observations weren't precise enough to tell the two models apart. The geocentric model was rather complicated, but for this question we can imagine it as saying that Earth is in the center of the universe, and the stars and planets go in circles around Earth in the order shown below:

Venus is the third circle from Earth and the sun is the fourth.

Part A. A DVD is a disk used to store digital data. They're often used to hold movies or video games.

By Marcin Sochacki (Wanted) - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=3749407

The digital data is stored in a long sequence of bumps on the bottom of the DVD. The bumps are all about the same size, and run in a spiral around the DVD.

http://www.futurekids.com.sg/doyouknow.html

Computers and video game consoles can use a device called a DVD player to read the sequence of bumps on the DVD.

Greg Krumm, "See Through DVD Drive", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8fqr-Fsl9xk

There are roughly $$10^{10}$$ bumps on a DVD. They're too small to see individually with your naked eye, but a DVD player can detect them using a laser.

The DVD player shines a laser onto the DVD from below (red cylinder in the image below). The laser light bounces off the DVD, where it enters the DVD player's detector (blue cylinder). The detector can use the reflected light to read the pattern of bumps on the DVD and send the information to a computer, which can then turn the data into a movie or video game.

The DVD player reads the bumps by following the DVD's spiral pattern. It starts near the center of the DVD and ends at the outside edge.

To follow the spiral, the DVD player has two motions. First, it spins the DVD. This brings new bumps over the laser. You can see the spinning motion in the gif above.

Second, the laser itself moves slowly outward as the DVD spins. This allows it to read tracks further toward the edge of the DVD as it advances along the spiral. The tracks of the spiral are all about the same thickness, so the distance of the laser from the center of the DVD is proportional to the number of rotations the DVD has made.

The DVD player needs to move the bumps past the laser at a constant number of bumps per second.

What is the relationship between $$\omega$$ and $$(t+t_0)$$ for the DVD player described in part (A)?

**note** We're finding a relationship between $$\omega$$ and $$(t+t_0)$$ instead of $$\omega$$ and $$t$$ because strict proportionalities like $$a \propto b^\alpha$$ imply that when $$b = 0,$$ $$a$$ is either zero or infinite (depending on the sign of $$\alpha$$). Here, because of the area with no bumps at the center, $$\omega$$ starts at some finite value when $$t = 0.$$ Making $$\omega$$ proportional to a power of $$(t + t_0)$$ corrects for the area with no bumps.

You can solve the problem by imagining the DVD has bumps all the way to the center, finding the proportionality between $$\omega$$ and $$t$$ in that case, and using it as the proportionality between $$\omega$$ and $$(t+t_0).$$

statement:
Part A. We've had several applications so far where we want to find the signed area between a curve and the horizontal axis.

For a graph that's a straight line, a semi-circle, or some other simple shapes, we can find this area with basic geometry. But if the graph plots some complicated real-world data, we won't be able to find a simple formula for the area.

Finding the signed area is a mathematical problem called __integration__.

Today, scientists mostly use computers to estimate this area, for example by cutting the area into many small rectangles and counting how many rectangles there are.

However, people needed to solve this problem before the modern computer age.

An early solution was to use an __analog computer__. You may have heard that computers, at their core, represent everything in terms of a series of 1's and 0's, called bits. This is true of __digital__ computers. Your home desktop, smart phone, calculator, etc. are all digital computers.

Analog computers are able to represent values continuously, not just using $$1$$ and $$0.$$

We will look at an analog computer very similar to the friction drive we studied in class. Analog computers similar to these were used as early as 1886. They solved problems such as predicting the tides and calculating the trajectories of missiles. They were mostly phased out in the 1950s and 1960s, when technological breakthroughs made digital computers hundreds of times faster and more reliable.

A simple analog computer is called a "ball and disk integrator". It begins with a sphere above a rotating disk. The sphere can be moved around so that it's either close to the center or close to the edge of the disk. The gif below shows the ball getting gradually closer to the center.

Veritasium, "The Most Powerful Computers You've Never Heard Of", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IgF3OX8nT0w

What happens to the angular speed of the ball throughout this gif? You can assume the angular speed of the disk is constant.

it is constant

it increases

it decreases

Part B. In the ball and disk integrator, the ball is connected to a roller. The roller turns in the opposite direction as the ball, with an angular speed proportional to the ball's. The roller is attached to a gear that moves a pen up or down on a piece of graph paper.

The $$y$$ location of the end of the pen is proportional to how far the gear at the end of the roller has spun in total since the beginning of running the analog computer. Therefore, the $$y$$ location of the end of the pen is also proportional to the total angular displacement of the ball.

name: Part A. This gif seems to show a helicopter taking off without spinning its blades:
desc: Part A. This gif seems to show a helicopter taking off without spinning its blades: ViralHog, "Helicopter Rises Without Moving Its Rotor", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jWIcVP6GRfw The blades really are spinning; the video simply looks as if they are not. If you were there…
statement:
Part A. This gif seems to show a helicopter taking off without spinning its blades:

ViralHog, "Helicopter Rises Without Moving Its Rotor", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jWIcVP6GRfw

The blades really are spinning; the video simply looks as if they are not. If you were there in-person, you wouldn't see the effect. The blades would appear to be rotating normally. Also, if someone else recorded the helicopter with a video, the blades might appear to spin in that video, especially if they used a high-speed video camera.

The blades appear stationary in this particular video because videos are a series of photographs taken at a certain frequency, and that frequency can match the frequency of rotation of the blades.

For example, imagine that the blades spin with a frequency of $$20 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ and that a camera is also taking video at a rate of $$20 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ Then the blades will spin all the way around between frames of the video. The blades will be in the same position each time the camera takes a picture, and in the video, it will look like the blades aren't spinning.

This effect is very common in videos of quickly-rotating or quickly-oscillating objects. It is called __aliasing__.

Aliasing does not necessarily make rotating objects appear to be stationary. It can also make them appear to be rotating, but with a different angular speed or direction than their true rotation. For example, videos of cars driving often look as if the wheels are rotating backwards.

Robbie Gonzalez, https://www.gizmodo.com.au/2016/05/why-do-wheels-sometimes-appear-to-spin-backwards/

(There is an extra complication with some wheels, or with the helicopter. The helicopter in the gif has five blades. If the blades each make just one fifth of a full rotation between frames of the video, then the video will still look as if the blades are not moving because the blades switch places with each other between frames, and the blades all look the same. Likewise, the wheel on a car may only have to rotate through a small angular displacement $$\theta$$ to look as if it has not rotated at all, so aliasing can set in at much lower frequencies. The wheel in the gif above appears to be rotating backward if you look at the spokes, but forward if you look at the cap in the center because the fraction of a rotation needed for the wheel to appear not to have moved is different between the spokes and hub. For this problem, assume we're looking at a wheel where all parts of the wheel have been painted differently, so the wheel only looks the same after one complete rotation.)

Suppose that a camera takes video at $$30.0 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ and that a wheel is spinning at a frequency of $$29.9 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ What will the video of the wheel appear to show?

Assume that the frequencies of both the camera and the wheel are perfectly constant. Frequencies are considered positive regardless of the direction the wheel rotates.

Select one of (a) through (d) and one of (e) through (g).

the wheel will appear not to move at all

the wheel will appear to oscillate back and forth

the wheel will appear to spin forward

the wheel will appear to spin backward

the apparent frequency of the wheel will be $$0.1 \;\mathrm{Hz}$$

the apparent frequency of the wheel will be $$29.95 \;\mathrm{Hz}$$

the apparent frequency of the wheel will be $$59.9 \;\mathrm{Hz}$$

Part B. This gif is from a video of a spinning top:

Although the top is spinning normally, it can appear to stop and even change direction in the video. You may have seen similar effects in movies, where the wheels of a car appear to change which direction they're spinning. You may even be able to see the effect in real life if you spin a top or fidget spinner under lights that flicker faster than your eyes can see. Some LEDs and fluorescent lights do this; you can find them in bathrooms more often than other rooms. In this problem, you'll work on understanding why this happens and relate it to rotational kinematics.

Imagine you make a video of a toy top spinning. Originally, the top is spinning with a frequency exactly double the frequency of your video, but friction and air drag slow it down steadily (with constant angular acceleration). You're supporting the top so that it can't fall over or wobble around; it simply spins more and more slowly until it stops. Then the top will spin completely twice around between each picture taken for the video, and the top will be in the same position in each picture. When you look at the video, the top will appear not to be moving.

However, in real life, tops spin more slowly over time. This means the top won't continue to look as if it's frozen. The video will look like the top has begun spinning, even though in real life it was already spinning, and is now just spinning a little slower.

Let's assume your top is painted a pattern that has no symmetry, so that it only appears to be in the same position after making one full rotation.

Make a plot of the apparent angular speed of the top $$\omega_a,$$ as seen in the video, over time $$t.$$ For this plot, assume that the frequency of the video is $$10 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ This means the video shows $$10$$ pictures each second. The original frequency of the top is $$20 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ meaning it spins all the way around $$20$$ times per second. Let the angular acceleration of the top be $$\alpha = 1.0 \;\mathrm{rad \cdot s}^{-2}$$ in the direction that slows the top's rotation down. $$\omega_a$$ should be measured in $$\mathrm{rad \cdot s^{-1}}\,.$$

Assume that the angular acceleration of the top is constant.

You may need a definition of how to find the angular speed of the top in a video. Assume angular speed is found in the following way: Comparing frames $$n$$ and $$n+1$$ of the video, the top will have rotated through an angular displacement $$\Delta \theta.$$ However, it is not possible to tell apart any two values of $$\Delta \theta$$ separated by an integer multiple of $$2\pi.$$ For example, if the true rotation of the top is $$\Delta \theta = 4.25 \pi$$ between the frames, then the first $$4\pi$$ angular displacement spins the top all the way around twice, which isn't visible, and it will look as if $$\Delta \theta_a = 0.25 \pi.$$

(Here we use $$\Delta \theta_a$$ for the apparent angular displacement of the top, as seen in the video.)

To find what the apparent angular displacement $$\Delta \theta_a$$ is, subtract multiples of $$2\pi$$ from the true angular displacement until the value is less than $$\pi$$ and use this as the angular displacement. This means $$\Delta \theta_a$$ is sometimes negative. For example, a true rotation of $$\Delta \theta = 1.9 \pi$$ will have $$\Delta \theta_v = 1.9 \pi - 2\pi = -0.1 \pi.$$

The apparent angular speed $$\omega_a$$ is equal to the apparent angular displacement between frames divided the time between frames.

We have not discussed the concept of __angular velocity__ yet, so we don't have negative values available to us yet. The angular speed is always positive by definition.

To indicate direction of rotation, label on your plot where the top appears to spin the same direction as the real rotation and where it appears to spin the opposite direction.

Turn in your plot with labeled axis and labels showing the forward and backward directions of rotation. You don't need a written explanation for this problem.

Part C. When a microphone records audio, it captures the pressure in the air over and over at times spaced slightly apart. The rate that the microphone makes readings is called its __sampling rate__, and can be measured in hertz. This is very similar to how a video camera takes a picture over and over at times spaced slightly apart. The rate the camera takes pictures is called its __frame rate__ and can also be measured in hertz.

Microphones record sound, which is an oscillation of the air. Since oscillations are periodic just like rotations, aliasing affects audio recordings just like it affects videos of rotating disks.

If we came up with formulas for the apparent frequency $$f_a$$ of a disk rotating at a true frequency $$f$$ and being recorded in a video taken at a frame rate $$f_v,$$ then those same formulas would accurately describe the frequency of the apparent frequency $$f_a$$ of a sound we hear in an audio recording as a function the true sound frequency $$f$$ and the sample rate $$f_s,$$ as long as we make the substitutions

$$\begin{aligned} \text{video } & \to \text{ audio} \\ f_a & \to f_a \\ f & \to f \\ f_v & \to f_s \end{aligned}$$

Microphones typically have sampling rates of either $$f_s = 44.10 \;\mathrm{KHz}$$ or $$48.00 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$ These sampling rates are set high enough so that there will be no aliasing for any sound within the range audible to humans.

An audio engineer makes a recording with a sample rate of $$f_{s1} = 44.10 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$ When she listens to the recording, she hears a sound playing back with a frequency of $$f_{a1} = 11.33 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$

She suspects there is a very high-pitched buzz in the recording studio making a sound at a frequency higher than humans can hear. She makes a new recording at the sampling rate $$f_{s2} = 48.00 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$ This time, there is still an unexplained sound, but its apparent frequency is $$f_{a2} = 15.23 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$

Assuming both unexplained sounds are aliasing of the same sound in the recording studio, what is the true frequency $$f$$ of the sound in the recording studio?

You can assume $$f < 1 \;\mathrm{MHz}.$$

Part A. In projectile motion, we may want to solve the problem of finding the angle $$\theta$$ that a projectile should be launched at in order to have it travel a horizontal distance $$d$$ before returning to the same height it was launched from. In this problem, we do not assume that the speed $$v_0$$ at launch is fixed.

The angle $$\theta$$ is called the __angle of reach__ given a target distance $$d,$$ launch speed $$v_0,$$ and gravitational acceleration $$g.$$

Which of the following is a plot of the angle of reach $$\theta$$ versus $$v_0$$ for a fixed $$d>0$$ and $$g>0?$$

Ignore air resistance in this problem.

Part B. In projectile motion, $$\theta, d,$$ and $$v_0$$ can all realistically vary. It can therefore be useful to understand $$\theta,$$ the angle of reach, as a function of __both__ $$d$$ and $$v_0.$$

One way we could do this is by taking the curve from part (A) as a starting point. This curve shows $$\theta$$ as a function of $$v_0,$$ with a fixed $$d.$$ We could then draw more curves on the same plot, each for a different value of $$d.$$

Alternatively, we could first draw a single curve for $$\theta$$ versus $$d,$$ given a fixed $$v_0.$$ Here is one such curve, using $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and a $$v_0$$ which you can calculate, if you find it helpful.

Then we could choose different values of $$v_0$$ and draw new $$\theta$$ versus $$d$$ curves, one for each value of $$v_0.$$ We can also add a A __legend__ is also called a __key__. It's the box on the side that tells you what each different curve means..

Which choice below shows what such a plot looks like?

All the plots use $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

(A)

Part C. One more way to represent the dependence of $$\theta$$ on both $$d$$ and $$v_0$$ at the same time is with a __contour plot__.

This is a plot on which __both__ axes represent independent variables. In this case, there will be one $$d$$ axis and one $$v_0$$ axis, since $$\theta$$ is a dependent variable that depends on the independent variables $$d$$ and $$v_0.$$

Each point on this plot represents a choice of both $$d$$ and $$v_0.$$ For example, point 1 below represents $$d = 6 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$v_0 = 15 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

There are two possible angles of reach at this point. (Most points on the plot have two angles of reach.) We will take the lower angle for this problem, ignoring the higher angle whenever there are two angles of reach.

To complete the plot, we draw a series of lines or curves, called __contours__. These lines or curves connect points on the plot that have the same value of $$\theta.$$

For example we could calculate the angle of reach $$\theta_1$$ at point 1 shown above. Then we could calculate the angle of reach at a few other places on the plot. Any time we found another point where the angle of reach was $$\theta_1,$$ we would plot that point. This would give us a series of points that form some shape on the plot. We could connect those points to form a curve. That curve is the contour $$\theta = \theta_1.$$

Then we could find contours for other values of $$\theta$$ and plot them as well. Finally, we could add labels or a legend to the plot to help us interpret the contours.

-------------------------

Let's look at two examples of contour plots to understand them better before you find contour plots for projectile motion.

You may have already seen __topographical maps__ or __contour maps__.

source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contour_line

The lower map is a topographical map. A map like this tells you the elevation using contours. Each line connects points with the same elevation.

Thought of as a contour plot, a topographical map treats latitude and longitude as independent variables, so there is one on each axis. It treats elevation as a dependent variable. The curves on the lower plot connect points with the same elevation.

As a second example, consider the formula $$ T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$$ for the period $$T$$ of a mass $$m$$ on a spring $$k.$$

To make a plot of $$T$$ as a function of both $$m$$ and $${}k,$$ we can construct a contour plot using $$m$$ and $${}k$$ as independent variables. (It doesn't matter which is horizontal and which is vertical.) The contours connect points that lead to the same period.

The contour map for $$T$$ looks like this:

$$T$$ increases moving up and to the left on this plot. Moving up corresponds to increasing $$m.$$ A higher mass takes longer to oscillate. Moving left corresponds to decreasing $${}k.$$ The lower the spring constant, the longer the period.

To construct this map, we found $$m = \left(\dfrac{T}{2\pi}\right)^2 \cdot k$$ meaning that for a fixed $$T,$$ $$m$$ versus $${}k$$ is a straight line, and the slope is proportional to $$T^2.$$

-----------------------

You may be wondering about the difference between the contour plots introduced here and the plots from part (B).

In this problem, we are interested in finding and representing the angle of reach, $$\theta.$$ We therefore think of $$\theta$$ as the dependent variable, and think of $$d$$ and $$v_0$$ as independent variables.

In part (B), we constructed plots where each curve represented different values of an __independent__ variable; each curve was a different value of $$v_0.$$

Here in part (C), we are looking at plots where each curve represents a different value of the __dependent__ variable; each curve is a different value of $$\theta.$$

If we instead wanted to solve the problem of the speed $$v_0$$ needed to launch a projectile, given the desired angle and range, the plots in part (B) would be contour plots.

In the topographical map example, the equivalent to part (B)'s plots would be to plot elevation versus longitude, and then to draw different curves representing different latitudes. This plot would be harder to interpret during a hike than the topographical map, although they represent the same information. ---------
