desc: Part A. Commercial airplanes can fly around $$90\%$$ the speed of sound, which is around $$300 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at $$10 \;\mathrm{km}$$ altitude. Most jets don't fly faster than about $$90\%$$ the speed of sound because the aerodynamics of flight near the speed of sound are…
statement:
Part A. Commercial airplanes can fly around $$90\%$$ the speed of sound, which is around $$300 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at $$10 \;\mathrm{km}$$ altitude. Most jets don't fly faster than about $$90\%$$ the speed of sound because the aerodynamics of flight near the speed of sound are fundamentally different than at lower speeds, and are very challenging.

There are airplanes that fly faster than the speed of sound, including military jets and a very small number of commercial airliners. Airplanes designed for supersonic (faster-than-sound) flight need to have very high power output, need to resist heating up due to compressing the air they fly through, and need to minimize their drag. Supersonic airliners need longer runways than normal jets because their liftoff speeds are higher due to their smaller wings. They also continuously produce a __sonic boom__ as they fly, which prevents them from flying over populated areas at low altitude. As a result, although supersonic flight for commercial jets is possible, it is very expensive. For the most part, airlines haven't found the cost of buying and maintaining supersonic airliners worthwhile.

Helicopters, unlike planes, don't fly close to the speed of sound. The fastest helicopters only fly around $$90 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ or about $$30\%$$ the speed of sound.

The main factor limiting helicopters' speed is that their __blades__ will travel near the speed of sound long before the helicopter itself gets near the speed of sound. When some part of a helicopter blade approaches the speed of sound, changes in the aerodynamics usually cause severe vibrations in the blade that engineers have not been able to overcome.

The tips of the blades of a helicopter travel faster than the helicopter itself, so if a helicopter were to fly $$90\%$$ the speed of sound, like a commercial jet, parts of its blades would travel faster than the sound barrier. This is not currently something helicopters can do.

Additionally, what matters is not the speed of the blades relative to the helicopter, but relative to the air. This is different on different sides of the helicopter.

https://aviation.stackexchange.com/questions/33596/how-does-wind-speed-affect-helicopter-rotor-speed

This creates another problem for helicopters. The blades that move faster relative to the air generate more __lift__, meaning they push the helicopter up more. If the right and left hand sides of the helicopter produce significantly different amount of lift, it will tip the helicopter over and make stable flight impossible.

Helicopters can adjust for this problem by changing the __angle of attack__ of the blades. This is the angle that the blades are inclined relative to the horizontal plane they rotate in.

LearnEngineering.org

Up to a certain limit (which real helicopters do not reach), increasing the angle of attack increases the lift.

Helicopters adjust the angle of attack of the blades continuously, going up and down one per revolution of the blades. This strategy is called __blade flapping__.

How should a helicopter engineer design the blade flapping of a helicopter? Use the helicopter pictured above - one going forward with blades rotating counterclockwise.

use the highest angle of attack when blades are on the left and lowest when they are on the right

use the highest angle of attack when the blades are either on the left or right, and the lowest when they are furthest forward or backward

use the highest angle of attack when the blades are either furthest foward or backward, and lowest when they are on the left or right

keep the angle of attack constant

Part A. In this multi-part problem, we'll explore a new mathematical fact related to the center of mass: Pappus' theorem.

----------------------------

Imagine taking a square with side lengths $$s$$ and rotating it one full rotation about an axis along one of the sides of the square.

As the square rotates, we keep track of all the space it passes through. This space is a cylinder with radius $$s$$ and height $$s.$$

The cylinder is called the __solid of revolution__ of the square about that axis.

Part B. The volume of a solid of revolution is called the __volume of revolution__.

Let's again take the example of a square revolved around one side.

The volume of revolution is the volume of the cylinder, $$\begin{aligned} V & = \text{(base area)} \cdot \text{height} \\ {} & = (\pi s^2) \cdot s \\ {} & = \pi s^3 \end{aligned}$$

----------------------------

Next we'll look at a different shape. This time, we move the square away from the axis of rotation, so the center of the square is a distance $$r$$ from the axis of rotation, as shown below.

Which is the correct equation for the volume of revolution of this square about this axis?

$$V = \pi r^2 \cdot s$$

$$V = \pi s^3$$

$$V = \pi \left(r-\dfrac12 s\right)^2 \cdot s$$

$$V = \pi \left(\left(r + \dfrac12s\right)^2 - \left(r - \dfrac12 s\right)^2\right)\cdot s$$

$$V = \pi \left((r+s)^2 - r^2\right)\cdot s$$

Which of the following is an interpretation of the result?

Part D. The interpretation you chose in part (C) is something we've only shown for the case of a square revolved around an axis parallel to one side of the square.

We'd like to know whether the same interpretation applies to any sort of volume of revolution, for example this circle:

To make an argument that it does, we try breaking the shape down into many small squares of side length $$s.$$

To find the volume of revolution of the entire shape, we can find the volume of revolution of each small square, then add them all up.

The goal of this part of the problem is to write an equation expressing this "add up all the squares" process. We can do that with __summation notation__.

Below is a brief example of summation notation. You can read more about summations at the following AoPS Wiki pages: https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/Sigma_notation https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/Summation

We found in the handout that the center of mass of this shape can be defined by

$$\vec{R} = \lim_{s\to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i = 1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i$$

In this equation, we label the squares with a number:

When $$i = 17,$$ for example, we look at this square:

That square has mass $$m_{17}$$ and position vector $$\vec{r}_{17}.$$ The next square has mass $$m_{18}$$ and position vector $$\vec{r}_{18},$$ etc.

The expression $$\sum_{i = 1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i$$ means that we take $$m \vec{r}$$ for each square and add them all together (using vector addition).

$$M$$ is the total mass of a shape.

The part $$\lim_{s\to 0}$$ means that there is some slight error when we approximate a shape by a bunch of squares, due to the edges having partial squares. If we cut the shape into smaller and smaller squares, the square shape gets closer and closer to the original shape, so the error gets smaller and smaller. A formal definition of limits is notoriously challenging. It was almost 200 years between the foundation of calculus, by Isaac Newton, Gottfried Leibniz, and others, until Karl Weierstrass first used the modern definition of a limit. When we need to discuss a limit, we will stick with an intuitive notion of "what the function goes towards". In this case, the quantity calculated using squares of side length $$s$$ goes toward the true center of mass, and not toward any other number as $$s$$ gets smaller.

If we want to break the center of mass into components, we have $$\begin{aligned} R_x & = \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i = 1}^n m_i r_{xi} \\ R_y & = \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i = 1}^n m_i r_{yi} \end{aligned}$$

Part E. Wen is a physics student who enjoys working on algebraic derivations. Wen arrives at this equation for a volume of revolution:

$$ V = \lim_{s \to 0} \sum_i 2\pi r_i s^2$$

Wen worked on this formula for some time, trying to understand what it meant and how it related to simple cases of volumes of revolution that he understood without the formula.

After a many false starts and failed attempts, Wen finally found some algebraic steps he was satisfied with, and wrote them down as a summary of his work.

First, Wen assumed that the figure he is revolving has a A __surface density__ is a mass per unit area of a surface. This is like a normal density, but in two dimensions instead of three of $$\lambda,$$ so that the total mass of the entire plane shape (not the solid of revolution) is $$M = \lambda A$$ where $$A$$ is the area of the shape being revolved.

Also, the mass of a square of side length $$s$$ is $$m = \lambda s^2$$

Wen then wrote down the following manipulations to his volume formula, all of which are algebraically valid:

$$\begin{aligned} V & = \lim_{s \to 0} \sum_i 2\pi r_i s^2 \\ {} &= \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \sum_i \lambda r_i s^2 \\ {} &= \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \sum_i m_i r_i \\ {} &= \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda A} A \sum_i m_i r_i \\ {} &= A \cdot 2\pi \left(\lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i r_i\right) \\ \end{aligned}$$

Below are a few different situations. In each, we could imagine trying to use momentum conservation to make predictions, but momentum conservation only holds when no momentum enters or leaves the system of study.

Each situation defines a system, then "inputs", meaning measurements or data we could use to make calculations with momentum, and then a "prediction", meaning a value that we want to calculate using momentum conservation.

**Select the situation in which assuming the momentum of the system is conserved would help make accurate and useful predictions for the behavior of the system.** (There is only one.)

The predictions do not have to be __perfectly__ accurate, since no predictions ever are. However, there is a large gap here between systems where momentum conservation makes largely-accurate predictions and systems where its predictions are very far off.

**(a)** A highway engineer is trying to design safer roads. They are studying the collision that happens when a car suddenly stops, and a large truck that was following the car hits its brakes, but cannot stop in time and hits the car, then they skid together down the road some distance before stopping. **system**: truck and car **inputs**: masses of truck and car, distance between stopped car and truck, initial velocity of truck **prediction**: velocity of car and truck after sliding $$50 \;\mathrm{m}$$ down the road after the collision

**(b)** An astrophysicist is studying a __galaxy merger__, the collision of two galaxies in deep space. International Gemini Observatory / NOIRLAB / NSF / AURA, retrieved https://www.cbsnews.com/news/galaxies-stunning-photo-cosmic-collision-milky-way/ Usually, stars don't literally slam into each other in a galaxy merger, since there is so much space between the stars, but the galaxies do interact via gravity, and can combine into one larger galaxy this way. The answer to this problem would be the same whether stars collide or not, though! The two galaxies are far away from other galaxies, and not influenced significantly by anything other than each other. **system**: the two galaxies combined **inputs**: the masses and velocities of all the stars (and all the other matter) in the galaxies **prediction**: the velocity of the center of mass of the combined galaxy after the merger

**(c)** A biomechanist is studying the flight of birds. They want to know how birds go from flying full speed ahead to landing safely on a perch.

https://www.quantamagazine.org/geometric-analysis-reveals-how-birds-mastered-flight-20220803/

**system**: bird **inputs**: mass and velocity of bird when $$10 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away from perch **prediction**: mass and velocity of bird when $$1 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ away from perch

statement:
Part A. Light has no mass, but it still has momentum.

The formula $$p = mv$$ for the momentum of a particle indicates that if the mass of the particle is zero, so is its momentum. However, physicists have found that the concept of momentum is more important than the specific formula for it we've used. Light can collide with things and push on them, for example, a phenomenon called __radiation pressure__. Scientists found new equations that accurately modeled radiation pressure, and decided to call the new mathematical construct "momentum", replacing the old construct of $$p = mv.$$

The new models scientists built for the momentum of light belong to the theory of special relativity. The equations of these models are extremely close to the equation $$p = mv$$ for objects traveling slowly compared to the speed of light, but as the speed increases, the equations become more and more different.

There is a simple equation for the momentum $$p$$ of light with energy $$E.$$ This formula gives the same type of momentum as the formula $$p=mv,$$ which it must since momentum from light can be converted into momentum in massive objects during collisions.

The speed of light is $$c.$$

Which of these equations could be the relation between $$p, c,$$ and $$E$$ for light?

$$p = Ec$$

$$p = E^2 c$$

$$p = c/E$$

$$p = Ec^2$$

$$p = E/c$$

statement:
Part A. There is a famous physics toy called __Newton's cradle__. It was invented by Isaac Newton's contemporary, French physicist Edme Mariotte.

The toy consists of a series of five balls suspended from wires:

Amazon.com

(The toy is sold with different numbers of balls, but we will assume there are five in this question.)

If you pull back one ball on the left and let it go, it will swing down, hit the remaining four balls, and stop. The three middle balls will not move. One ball will bounce up from the right hand side. When that ball comes back, the process will reverse. The rightmost ball will hit the four stationary balls and stop, and the leftmost ball (the one that was dropped originally) will bounce up into the air:

xmphysics, "Newton's Pendulum (Gangnam Style)" https://youtu.be/YB7KUGdP7wI

Our description is not perfect; the three middle balls do not remain completely stationary, for example. However, for this question, we'll idealize the behavior to say that they stay completely stationary and only the leftmost and rightmost balls move.

If you pull back two balls and release them, they'll again stop when they hit the remaining balls, and two balls will come out on the right. The middle ball remains (nearly) stationary:

The same works for more balls, e.g. here are three and four balls pulled back:

One can create more complicated patterns of bounces by pulling multiple balls back different distances before releasing them:

For this question, we'll focus on the case of pulling back one ball and releasing it to collide with four stationary balls. The result, as shown at the top of the question, is that the ball stops and one ball comes out the other side of the cradle with the same velocity as the incoming ball.

Some sources explain this observation by invoking momentum and kinetic energy. They say that if the collisions are modeled as elastic, then combining momentum and energy conservation, the only possibility is for the incoming ball to stop, and for one ball to come out on the other side.

We will examine whether this explanation of Newton's cradle is accurate and complete.

Suppose one ball approaches at speed $$v$$ from the left and that, as a hypothesis, that ball will stop, and two balls will pop out together from the right hand side at speed $$v_r.$$

What does $$v_r$$ need to be according to momentum conservation? What does it need to be according to kinetic energy conservation?

Give your answers as decimals to two decimal places.

mathjax: \begin{align*} \text{ according to momentum conservation,} \,\, v_r & = \blank v\\ \text{ according to kinetic energy conservation,}\,\, v_r & = \blank v \end{align*}

allowed: 1.023456789

Part B. In part (A), you should have found different answers for momentum and kinetic energy conservation.

Consider a few different claims about the meaning of this calculation.

**(a)** Aaron says: If someone throws the ball, they're putting energy into it, so the calculation based on kinetic energy conservation will give good predictions of experiments in that case. However, if the ball is simply moving before coming into the collision, it has momentum because of its mass and velocity, so the calculation based on momentum conservation will give accurate predictions.

**(b)** Bryn says: Momentum is conserved in collisions, but kinetic energy can be converted into thermal energy. The momentum-based calculation is the correct one to use, assuming that one ball stops and two come out. However, I'm not sure whether we can get Newton's cradle to actually do that.

**(c)** Chris says: The calculation shows that it's impossible to conserve both momentum and kinetic energy in this scenario. A good model for Newton's cradle is that both are conserved. If we do the experiment, we will not be able to get the incoming ball to stop and two balls to come out together on the right hand side.

**(d)** Deven says: I agree with Chris. This is a proof that, assuming momentum and energy conservation, when one ball comes in, it stops, and one ball comes out the other side. That's what we have already observed anyway!

**Which claims are correct?**

Select two. The claims do not have to be complete explanations to be correct. They only need to avoid saying things that are incorrect.

To judge whether claims are correct, you can continue assuming that gravity and influences from the strings are negligible during the collisions.

Elastic collisions are a good model for Newton's cradle, but don't count a claim as incorrect just because it speculates about using inelastic collisions as a model.

Part C. A different possibility for what could happen in Newton's cradle is that when one ball comes in from the left with velocity $$v,$$ it bounces back at velocity $$v_1,$$ while the remaining four balls move to the right together with velocity $$v_4.$$

Assuming momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved in the collision, what are $$v_1$$ and $$v_4$$ in terms of $$v?$$

Give your answers as decimals to two decimal places.

If it is not possible to conserve both momentum and kinetic energy in this type of collision, enter 0 for each.

mathjax: \begin{align*} v_1 & = \blank v \\ v_4 & = \blank v \end{align*}

allowed: -1.023456789

Part D. You have just done the calculation in part (C). There, we used momentum and energy conservation to calculate what happens when one ball approaches four stationary balls, but the result was different from experiment. Experiment shows that (to a good approximation), the incoming ball stops and one ball leaves from the right hand side.

Which of the following are accurate interpretations of the calculation and the experimental result?

Select all the correct interpretations.

**(a)** Because the calculation and experiment don't agree, and the calculation was based on momentum and energy conservation, either momentum is not conserved in the collisions or energy is not conserved in them.

**(b)** While elastic collisions that conserve momentum are a good model for Newton's cradle, they are not enough to determine what will happen. We would need to make additional modeling assumptions to match Newton's cradle experiments to theory.

**(c)** In part (C), we made strong assumptions about how the balls move, then calculated two velocities. If we allow all the balls to have any velocity before and after the collision, the real experimental result will be one possible solution to the momentum and energy conservation equations, but there will be many others.

**(d)** Because there are different ways to conserve both momentum and energy, Newton's cradle cannot be accurately modeled. It is one of the phenomena in science that can only be understood based on experimental evidence, not theory.

Part A. Here's a small steel ball bouncing off a hard surface:

Steve Mould, "Weird metal that's also glass is insanely bouncy", https://youtu.be/QpuCtzdvix4

Because the ball is small and light, and because both surfaces are hard, there is very little deformation of either the ball or surface during the bounce.

The ball always feels a gravitational force $$\vec{F}_{g; E \to B} = m \vec{g} = -mg \, \hat{y}$$ downward.

If the ball were to sit on the surface, it would feel a force $$mg\, \hat{y}$$ upward. This force would cancel the downward force from gravity so that the ball would not accelerate. This force is called the The word "normal" here means "perpendicular to". The force is perpendicular to the plane of the surface the ball is bouncing off. We write the normal force as $$\vec{F}_{N, S \to B}.$$ The $${}_N$$ indicates that it's a normal force. The $${}_{S \to B}$$ means it's a force from the surface to the ball.

Thus, if the ball sits on the surface without moving, we have

$$\begin{aligned} \vec{F}_{N; S \to B} & = - \vec{F}_{g; E \to B} \\ {} & = mg \, \hat{y} \end{aligned}$$

However, we only know this equation to model the ball sitting stationary on the surface.

When bouncing, the ball is accelerating because it changes from moving downward before the bounce to moving upward after the bounce. It makes this change over a short time.

The force that accelerates the ball during a bounce is the normal force from the surface.

How large is the magnitude $$F_{N; S \to B}$$ of the normal force during a bounce?

$$F_{N; S \to B} = 0$$

$$F_{N; S \to B} = mg$$

$$mg < F_{N; S \to B} \le 2 mg$$

$$2mg < F_{N; S \to B} \le 10 mg$$

$$10mg < F_{N; S \to B}$$

We could still find how high the ball is bouncing using a stopwatch. We'd time how long the ball is in the air for a single bounce, and then using equations of constant acceleration for free fall, we could find the height of the bounce.

Suppose that the video is not playing in real time. Instead, it is playing back at a rate $$\alpha$$ times real time, i.e., if $$\alpha = 2,$$ then the video is playing back twice as fast as real life, and if $$\alpha = \dfrac12,$$ it's playing back at half speed.

If $$\alpha \neq 1,$$ then our height estimate $$h_\alpha$$ would not equal the real height of the bounces, $$h.$$

Part C. The gif in part (A) doesn't have a high frame rate, and we can't see the details of the bouncing.

Suppose the gif did have a very high framerate, so that advancing frame by frame, we could tell for how many frames the ball was in contact with the surface, and how many frames long a bounce lasts.

However, we'll imagine that we still don't know the frame rate of the video. It is playing back at a rate $$\alpha$$ times the real rate.

We calculate the force on the ball in the following way:

1. We assume that $$\alpha = 1.$$ 2. We use the duration of a bounce to find how high the ball is bouncing. We call that $$h_\alpha.$$ 3. $$h_\alpha$$ provides a scale. We use this to determine the diameter $$D_\alpha$$ of the ball. 4. We know the ball is steel, so we assume its density is $$8 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$ and estimate its mass, $$m_\alpha.$$ 5. We use the height $$h_\alpha$$ of the bounce and $$g \approx 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ to find the velocity of the ball just before the bounce. 6. We use the $$\vec{v}_\alpha$$ and mass $$m_\alpha$$ of the ball to find its momentum just before the bounce. 7. We assume the bounce is elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved during the bounce. We use this to find the momentum change $$\Delta \vec{p}_\alpha$$ of the ball during the bounce. 8. Still assuming $$\alpha = 1,$$ we find the duration $$\Delta t_\alpha$$ of the bounce by going through the video frame by frame. 9. We use $$\vec{F}_{N; S \to B; \alpha} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}_\alpha}{\Delta t_\alpha}$$ to find the magnitude of the normal force from the surface on the ball during the bounce, assuming it is roughly constant during the bounce. We ignore gravitational force during the bounce because the bounce is so short that gravitational force is negligible.

All the quantities here have $$\alpha$$ subscripts because they are calculated using $$\alpha = 1,$$ and if $$\alpha \neq 1,$$ they may be incorrect. The correct values would be written $$h, D, m, \ldots$$ as opposed to our estimates $$h_\alpha, D_\alpha, m_\alpha, \ldots.$$

How do $$m$$ and $$m_\alpha$$ compare?

If the density of a ball is $$\rho,$$ its mass is $$\rho V = \rho \cdot \dfrac43 \pi r^3.$$

statement:
Consider an Atwood machine in which each mass is attached to a spring.

We will assume that $$m_B > m_A.$$

The springs are identical. The more force a spring has to exert on a box it's attached to, the more it will have to stretch to do it. __Hooke's law__ states that $$\Delta \ell,$$ the amount that the spring has been stretched, is proportional to the force the spring exerts.

The springs are significantly damped, so that the masses will quickly stop oscillating after the masses are released.

Model the rope, springs, and pulley as massless, and ignore any friction or air drag in the pulley or on the boxes.

Once the springs stop oscillating, but while the Atwood machine is still accelerating, which spring will be longer?

Explain your reasoning.

By analyzing the potential and kinetic energy, we have previously found that the acceleration of an Atwood machine has magnitude $$a = \dfrac{(m_B - m_A)g}{m_B + m_A}$$

You can use this fact without proving it in your response.

Each box experiences a force from gravity and a force from the spring. You will have to account for both these forces. Newton's second law for the system of one box applies to the vector sum of the two forces on that box. I.E. $$\vec{F}_{g; E \to A} + \vec{F}_{s\to A} = m_A \vec{a}_A,$$ and likewise for box $$B.$$ Here $$\vec{F}_{s\to A}$$ is the force from the spring on box $$A.$$

ChatGPT is very good at writing complete, coherent sentences, but its understanding of physics is sometimes a bit shaky. In fact, if given the same prompt multiple times, it will contradict itself.

Breaking ChatGPT's response down into claims, we have

**b)**"The kinetic energy of an object is given by the formula KE = 1/2mv^2"

**c)** "they will both reach the same final velocity."

**d)** "the boxes will not have the same momentum"

**e)** "momentum is mass times velocity"

**f)** "the two boxes have different masses"

**Select the claim which is incorrect.**

Part A. In the handout, we discussed lifting a book of mass $$m$$ a distance $$\Delta y.$$

There, we imagined a portion of the lift during which the force we applied to the book was constant and we lifted the book at constant velocity $$v.$$ We'll call this "gentle" lifting, and give it the subscript $$G.$$ In gentle lifting, the force was $$\vec{F}_{H \to B; G} = - m \vec{g}$$ where $$H \to B$$ means "from the hand, to the book."

The work done by the hand on the system of the book and its gravitational interaction with Earth was $$W_{H \to B; G} = mg \Delta y$$

The book gained gravitational potential energy $$\begin{aligned} \Delta U_G & = W_{H \to B; G}\\ {} & = mg \Delta y \end{aligned}$$

It is also possible to lift the book with a larger force. We'll call this "violent" lifting, and give it the subscript $$V.$$ Suppose you lift the book a distance $$\Delta y$$ using violent lifting with constant force $$\vec{F}_{H \to B;V} = -1.5 m \vec{g} $$

Your hand does some work $$W_{H \to B; V}$$ in this case, and the gravitational potential energy of the book increases by some amount $$\Delta U_V.$$

Select the **two** of the following statements, equations, or inequalities about work, energy, acceleration, and velocity are correct descriptions of violent lifting.

Although the book might continue moving after reaching the height change $$\Delta y,$$ ignore any further motion, and answer just for the period during which the book undergoes a height change $$\Delta y.$$

$$W_{H \to B;V} > W_{H \to B;G}$$

$$\Delta U_{V} > \Delta U_G$$

The book continuously gains kinetic energy in violent lifting, but not in gentle lifting.

The book has kinetic energy in violent lifting, but not in gentle lifting.

statement:
Part A. Below is Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen running.

https://www.facebook.com/ingebrigtsenjakob/photos/a.975757819230692/1380573998749070/?type=3

Ingebrigtsen also frequently runs on treadmills.

https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=218821882501882

Some people have an intuition that a treadmill belt "pulls" your feet along, making it easier to run at a given pace. Others believe running on treadmills and running outside are largely the same. In this problem, we'll examine running both outside and on a treadmill from the point of view of work and energy.

We can assume that Ingebrigtsen's foot does not slip relative to whatever surface he is running on. This means that, when running outside, the velocity of the bottom of his shoe is zero while it touches the ground. (Ingebrigtsen's center of mass continues moving forward even though his shoe's velocity is zero. His shoe, foot, and leg fall behind for a while, and then he swings them forward to catch up while in the air and while the other leg is touching the ground. Running consists of doing this over and over, alternating legs.)

Likewise, when Ingebrigtsen runs on a treadmill, his shoe has the same velocity as the surface of the treadmill while he runs. (In real life, there is probably some small amount of slipping, but it is usually very small, and we will ignore it.)

The motion of running is quite complicated - many different body parts are moving simultaneously. We will assume that Ingebrigtsen is running a very even pace. If running outside, he takes essentially the same amount of time to run each hundred meters he travels. If running on a treadmill, he keeps the treadmill belt moving at constant speed. This means his time-averaged acceleration is close to zero. However, the horizontal component of force between his shoe and the belt is sometimes forward and sometimes backward.

Below is a sample plot of measurements of both the vertical force component $$F_V$$ and horizontal force component $$F_H$$ from a runner on the surface they are running on. The plot shows three strides.

Chang, Young-Hui, and Rodger Kram. "Metabolic cost of generating horizontal forces during human running." Journal of Applied Physiology 86.5 (1999): 1657-1662.

You can assume a plot of Ingebrigtsen's forces would be similar.

Consider Ingebrigtsen (along with his clothing and shoes) and his gravitational interactions with Earth as one system, the treadmill as another, and the air as a third.

For this part of the problem, assume that both the ground and the treadmill are flat.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

Answer each from the reference frame of the ground / floor.

Outside, Ingebrigtsen does positive work on the ground throughout his stride.

Outside, the ground does positive work on Ingebrigtsen throughout his stride.

Outside, Ingebrigtsen alternately does positive, then negative work on the ground at different parts of his stride.

On the treadmill, Ingebrigtsen does positive work on the ground throughout his stride.

On the treadmill, the ground does positive work on Ingebrigtsen throughout his stride.

On the treadmill, Ingebrigtsen alternately does positive, then negative work on the ground at different parts of his stride.

abc

new lines

left align

Part B. Suppose that the treadmill belt runs at constant speed and that we ignore air resistance.

Then according to the principle of relativity, we can analyze the treadmill from any reference frame.

Use this fact to help you choose all the correct statements below.

Running on the treadmill when it is flat is physically the same as running on a similar surface outside.

Running on the treadmill when it is flat is easier than running on a similar surface outside because the treadmill does work on you.

Running on the treadmill when it is inclined is physically the same as running up a similar incline on a similar surface outside.

Running on the treadmill when it is inclined is easier than running up a similar incline outside because you don't need to raise yourself up to a higher elevation when on the treadmill.

abc

new lines

left align

Part C. A significant difference between a treadmill and running outside is that there is very little wind resistance on a treadmill; we can model the wind resistance as zero on a treadmill.

Even if the air is still, there is still wind resistance when running outside because your body moves forward relative to the air, i.e, if Ingebrigtsen runs at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ outside, he experiences a headwind of $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ even when the air is still. When he runs at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ on a treadmill, he experiences effectively no wind resistance.

We have previously modeled the effect of wind resistance. Our model is equivalent to a force $$F_D = \dfrac12 C_D \rho A v^2$$ where $$F_D$$ is the magnitude of wind drag force an object feels, $$C_D$$ is its drag coefficient, $$\rho$$ is the density of air, $$A$$ is the object's cross-sectional area, and $$v$$ is the speed of the wind relative to the object.

To compensate for the lack of wind resistance on a treadmill, Ingebrigtsen could set the treadmill to an incline, making running more difficult in a way similar to how wind resistance makes running more difficult.

Treadmills measure inclines using "percentages." For example, a treadmill incline of $$1\%$$ means that if the treadmill belt is $$2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ long, it rises $$2 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ from back to front.

Suppose Ingebrigtsen wants to set the incline of the treadmill so that he exerts the same power to run at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ on the treadmill as he does running at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ outside. Assume that all factors aside from the wind resistance and incline of the treadmill are identical between outside and the treadmill.

What should the incline of the treadmill be?

You may use the following values:

$$\begin{aligned} C_D & = 0.9 \\ \rho & = 1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}\\ A & = 0.5 \;\mathrm{m}^2 \\ v & = 5 \;\mathrm{m/s} \\ m & = 65 \;\mathrm{kg} \\ g & = 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2} \end{aligned}$$

Give your answer to the nearest percent.

statement:
Particle physicists use large colliders to smash particles into each other, creating new particles. Large detectors are able to follow the paths that the newly-created particles take for a short time.

Below is the ATLAS detector at CERN.

By Maximilien Brice - http://cds.cern.ch/record/910381, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=47143612

Each of the eight large tubes around the detector is a powerful magnet. There are people in the photo; they can serve as a scale.

Particle detectors have strong magnetic fields in the region where the new particles are created. Particles with no electric charge (e.g. neutrons) are unaffected by magnetic fields, but particles with electric charge (e.g. electrons and protons) Note that we're saying __magnetic__ fields put force on __electric__ charges. The connection between electricity and magnetism may not seem very strong when we think about light bulbs or static discharge as representatives of electricity and refrigerator magnets or compasses as representatives of magnetism, but electric and magnetic fields are closely linked, and described together in a single mathematical theory. Electric fields also put forces on electric charges. This issue of "magnetic charges" is more complicated, and best left for a class dedicated to electricity and magnetism. from the magnetic field.

We can model force from the magnetic field on a particle with electric charge as always being perpendicular to the direction of motion of the charge, and to the magnetic field itself.

This situation is similar to that of gravitational force and circular orbits. There, the gravitational force is always perpendicular to the motion of the orbiting object.

Using this model of magnetic forces, what is the work done by the magnetic field on an electron when the electron makes one full circular orbit in the magnetic field?

statement:
Part A. A box sits stationary and undisturbed on a table.

generated by StableDiffusion

Svetlana is a student taking her first physics class. Although a box sitting on a table is a mundane scenario, she wants to study it anyway. Her goal is to improve the connection between her everyday intuition and the models, terminology, and equations she's been using in her class.

First, Svetlana thinks about the situation as if she had not taken physics at all. From this perspective, it doesn't seem to Svetlana that the table is doing anything to the box. The table doesn't get tired, or seem visibly affected by the box. At most, she intuitively thinks of the table as "getting in the box's way", or perhaps "supporting" the box, so it doesn't fall.

Svetlana then thinks about the box in terms of physics concepts. She considers

1. forces 2. energy 3. kinematics (e.g. velocity and acceleration)

She writes a summary of the box-table situation from each of these three perspectives.

Svetlana works in the reference frame of the table. She assumes the table is flat and horizontal.

Let's figure out Svetlana's conclusions for ourselves.

**According to the models of physics we've studied over this course, which one of the following is an accurate description of the box-table situation?**

Only select an option if the value discussed is non-zero. For example, choice (a) is "The table is exerting a normal force on the box." If you think of the table as exerting a normal force, but with magnitude zero, then do not select this option.

Do select an option if the value is negative. For example, choice (c) is "The table is doing work on the box." Select this even if you find that the table is doing negative work on the box.

Svetlana is mostly focused on the table's effect on the box, so we don't have choices related to force exerted by the box on the table, etc. That doesn't mean that force doesn't exist. It only means we aren't focused on that force in this problem.

The table is exerting a normal force on the box.

The table is exerting a friction force on the box.

The table is doing work on the box.

The box has velocity.

The box has acceleration.

abc

new lines

left align

Part B. Svetlana realizes that, according to her pre-physics intuition, the table doesn't react to the box. It's an inanimate object, and it is "doing nothing."

Nonetheless, Svetlana's analysis says that the table is "exerting force" on the box. She is confused; the table cannot be both "exerting a force" and "doing nothing."

Early in her physics class, Svetlana didn't worry about counterintuitive ideas. As a beginner, she realized she couldn't build a deep understanding all at once. She is good at algebra and focused on the mathematical calculations.

When she can blend her visualizations of the world with physics equations, vocabulary, and graphs, Svetlana thinks of it as having "physics intuition." She's now focusing on building this intuition up by taking counterintuitive ideas and breaking them down.

Svetlana finds a video by YouTuber Derek Muller The video is 2:24 long. It's linked to the left. You can watch the video, or skip the video and use the summary below. in intuitive terms.

In the video, Muller stands on the ground. An arrow pointing downward shows up above him, representing a gravitational force downward on his body, from the entire Earth. Then two upward arrows show up, one at each foot. These represent the a normal force upward on Muller from the ground beneath his feet.

Veritasium, "What Forces Are Acting on You?", YouTube

To explain how the inanimate ground exerts a force, Muller then steps on the spring-supported horse toy.

ibid.

As Muller stands on the horse, its spring compresses under his weight. The compressed spring pushes back up on Muller, and this push upward is the normal force.

Muller then explains:

The ground is very similar to this spring. The ground is just a very stiff spring. But every time you step, you compress the ground a little bit, and that is enough to make the ground create a force on you, pushing you back upwards. And the force of the ground upwards must be equal to the gravitational force downwards so that you stay at rest.

Svetlana wants to adapt Muller's explanation to the situation with a box on a table.

Which one of the following statements **__disagrees__** with Muller's explanation of normal force?

There is a normal force from the table on the box.

Although the table appears unaffected by the box, the box really does have an effect on the table.

The table is slightly compressed by the weight of the box.

The table is like a very stiff spring.

The magnitude of the normal force from the table on the box is larger than the magnitude of the gravitational force on the box.

If you were to pick the box up off the table, the shape of the table's surface would change (a tiny bit).

abc

new lines

left align

Part C. Svetlana thinks Muller's explanation makes some sense, but when she puts a box on a table, there's no visible deflection of the table.

Svetlana at first thinks of the idea that the ground or a table is "like a spring" as only an analogy, but not a meaningful real-world idea. She wonders whether the table really compresses a microscopic amount, or whether we're just supposed to think of it that way.

Svetlana takes a few meter sticks and uses them to make a bridge between two stacks of books. This forms a simple "table." She places a marshmallow on top the meter sticks. According to Muller's explanation, the meter sticks should be deflected downward by the marshmallow, but Svetlana doesn't see anything.

Next, Svetlana places a cell phone on the meter sticks, but still doesn't see a deflection. Then she puts a book on them, and thinks that maybe she sees a little bit of deflection. Eventually, she puts a bowling ball on the meter sticks, causing a large, obvious deflection.

Marc Reif, https://fysicsfool.wordpress.com/2017/07/09/a-physics-teachers-strongman-trick/

One interpretation is that even a marshmallow caused some deflection of the meter sticks, but it was too small to see. Another is that large, heavy objects cause a lot of deflection, medium objects cause a smaller deflection, but light objects like a marshmallow don't cause any real deflection of a meter stick, much less a sturdy table.

Similarly, Svetlana imagines pushing on a wall. She can imagine that when she presses against a flimsy wall, she deforms it, but finds it hard to imagine she can deform or compress a sturdy large wall or a heavy steel beam just by pressing lightly against them.

Svetlana finds a description of a demo to visualize the deflection of heavy walls, steel beams, tables, etc. The setup is shown below.

ibid.

A rod is connected to a heavy steel beam (called a "girder" in the photo). This way, if the steel beam deflects a tiny amount, it will push the rod.

A second rod, called a dowel, lies underneath the first rod at a right angle to it. If the beam deflects a small amount, it will push the rod connected to it. That will rotate the dowel through a small angle.

A mirror is attached to the dowel. The mirror will rotate a tiny bit along with the dowel.

Finally, a laser reflects a beam of light off the mirror, creating a spot of laser light on another wall on the opposite side of the room (not shown in picture).

To summarize, the idea is: - Svetlana will push on the steel beam with her hands - this will cause a microscopic deflection of the beam - the beam will push the first rod a little bit - the first rod will rotate the dowel a little bit - the dowel will rotate the mirror a little bit - rotating the mirror will change the reflection of the laser light - the dot of laser light on the far wall will move

The point of this system is that the laser light moves a much greater distance than any deflection of the beam. In fact, the dot of laser light can move tens of thousands of times further than the deflection of the beam, since even a small change in the angle of the mirror can result in a significant motion of the laser light after it travels across the entire room.

After acquiring some materials and building her own version of this setup, Svetlana pushes on the steel beam. As she pushes, she can see the laser light move.

ibid.

If Svetlana pushes on the beam three times (relaxing between pushes), the laser dot deflects three times.

If Svetlana leans against the beam, the laser dot deflects for a brief period while the wall is reacting, but once she is leaning steadily at equilibrium, the laser dot is back at its original location.

If Svetlana leans against the beam, as long as she continues leaning, the laser dot remains deflected from its original position, only going back when she stops leaning.

The harder Svetlana pushes against the beam, the more the laser dot deflects.

If Svetlana pulls outward on the beam, the laser dot deflects the opposite direction as it did when she pushed.

Svetlana's teacher explains that the atoms in a steel beam get closer together when the beam is compressed. The bonds between the atoms are so strong that the compression is slight, and we don't usually notice it unless we build the laser apparatus from part (C). She also says that different materials have bonds of different strength.

The model is intended to give a good approximation of how atoms and bonds work in materials, without necessarily being a perfect representation of every solid in every detail.

After thinking about this model, which one of the following is **__not__** a reasonable conclusion for Svetlana to draw about atoms, bonds, and solid materials?

In a solid, individual atoms can all jiggle around, and this explains where the solid stores thermal energy. If we heat the solid up, the jiggling will increase.

If we compress a solid from all sides, shrinking it, the atoms in the solid get closer to each other.

Different materials can be harder or easier to compress, based at least partially on the types of bonds between the atoms in the material.

Atoms in a solid maintain roughly the same neighbors over time. If atom A is right next to and bonded to atom B right now, they will likely still be right next to each other a short time later. They are not moving around at random all the time.

Every solid material has all its atoms in a perfect primitive cubical grid. Ignoring atoms on the surface, each atom makes exactly six bonds, one to a neighbor above, below, left, right, forward, and behind.

statement:
Our phrasing of Newton's three laws was:

**First Law:** If there are no external forces on a system, then the velocity of its center of mass will not change.

**Second Law:** The acceleration of the center of mass of a system and the net force on a system are related by $$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m \vec{a}_{\rm cm}$$ where $$m$$ is the total mass of the system.

**Third Law:** When systems $$A$$ and $$B$$ interact, there will be a force from system $$A$$ on system $$B$$ and a force from system $$B$$ on system $$A.$$ These forces are related by $$\vec{F}_{A \to B} = - \vec{F}_{B \to A}$$

Below is Isaac Newton's original phrasing of the three laws of motion (translated from Latin). They are presented in a random order.

**Description A** To every action, there is always opposed an equal reaction; or, the mutual actions of the two bodies upon each other are always equal, and directed to contrary parts.

**Description B** The change of motion of an object is proportional to the force impressed; and is made in the direction of the straight line in which force is impressed.

**Description C** Every body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed upon it.

statement:
Part A. This week, we'll work on the setup of an experiment to test Newton's second law. We'll conduct the experiment and analyze the results in next week's homework.

----------------

Below is a child's toy schoolbus. To use it, a child can pull it backward while keeping the wheels on the ground. When released, the schoolbus rolls forward.

This toy does not have batteries, an electric motor, etc.

The further back the child (or physicist) pulls the bus backwards, the further it travels forward across the floor when released.

Over this multi-part problem, we will work through an experiment to investigate the motion of the bus, and review some ideas about force and energy.

To begin, let's think about what the models of motion we've studied so far tell us about the operation of the bus.

Which one of the following statements about the bus agrees with our models of motion?

By conservation of energy, the bus cannot go forward further than it is pulled backward.

By Newton's third law, when a child pulls backward on the bus, the bus exerts a forward force on the child.

While a child is exerting a backward force and pulling the bus backward, friction from the floor is exerting a forward force on the bus. Because the bus is going backwards, we know that the child's force is greater than the friction force.

By conservation of momentum, the bus cannot go forward without something else going backward at the same speed.

The child exerts a backward force to pull the bus backward, and by Newton's third law, when the child releases the bus an equal and opposite forward force takes over to push the bus forward.

Part B. Inside the bus isThe actual spring inside the toy looks a little different than the springs we're used to, but model it as the type of spring we're used to for the purpose of this problem which does not necessarily obey Hooke's law. As the child pulls the bus backward, the spring gets compressed, storing elastic potential energy.

Inside the bus, gears and other mechanisms link the rotation of the wheels to the compression of the spring. The amount the spring is compressed is proportional to how far the bus is pulled back.

We pull the bus backward at constant velocity with a pulling force $$\vec{F}_{\rm pull}$$ that is parallel to the ground. The wheels do not slip.

At the same time that we exert force $$\vec{F}_{\rm pull},$$ the spring exerts a force $$\vec{F}_{\rm spring}$$ on the mechanism it's connected to.

What is the relationship between the magnitudes $$F_{\rm pull}$$ and $$F_{\rm spring}?$$

Ignore any friction forces and assume that no mechanical energy is lost.

You may want to briefly review the gif in part (A) while answering this question.

$$F_{\rm pull} = F_{\rm spring}$$

$$F_{\rm pull} < F_{\rm spring}$$

Part C. We would like to use the bus to test Newton's second law of motion, $$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m\vec{a}$$

We can add mass to the bus by placing items inside it. Then we can run the bus with varying amount of mass and observe the motion.

Friction from the ground will push the bus forward, but we don't know what the magnitude $$F_{\rm push}$$ of that friction force will be as the bus moves forward.

We decide to measure $$F_{\rm push}$$ before designing an experiment on Newton's second law.

Which one of these procedures would **not** let us determine the general shape of the force extension curve for the spring in the bus?

Assume each step is feasible. Judge only whether the procedure measures $$F_{\rm push}$$ or not.

**(a)** Take the spring out of the bus. Put it on the scale and If the weight of the spring is $$0.05 \;\mathrm{N},$$ the scale will read $$0.05 \;\mathrm{N}$$ when we put the spring on it. When we press down on the spring with $$0.10 \;\mathrm{N}$$ more force, the scale will read $$0.15 \;\mathrm{N},$$ so its reading is higher than the force we exert. Instead, we can put the spring on the scale, then press the "tare" button. The scale will read zero, and when we press down on the spring with $$10 \;\mathrm{N}$$ of force, the scale will read $$10 \;\mathrm{N}.$$with the spring uncompressed. Then press down on the top of the spring with varying forces.

For each force, record how much the spring is compressed and the reading on the scale. Take the scale readings as measurements of $$F_{\rm push}.$$

**(b)** Start the bus stationary on the floor. Push it backward a fixed distance using just our hands. Put the scale on the front of the bus, allowing the bus to push forward against the scale. Gradually pull the scale backwards. The bus will roll forward to continue pressing against the scale.

Stop periodically to read the scale and record how far the bus has rolled forward. Continue until the bus no longer pushes up against the scale. Use the scale readings at $$F_{\rm push}.$$

**(c)** Start the bus stationary on a table. Pull the bus backward a fixed distance. Set up a pulley at the edge of the table, and a box on a string of negligible mass hanging off the pulley. Tie the other end of the string to the back of the bus, resembling a half Atwood machine.

Allow the bus to move forward small amounts. Each time, stop the bus and adjust the mass in the box until it remains stationary, held by the tension in the string. After each measurement, record how far the bus has moved and use the scale to find the weight of the box. Take the weight of the box as $$F_{\rm push}.$$

Part D. To measure $$F_{\rm push},$$ we placed a kitchen scale in front of the bus. To secure the scale at a fixed angle, we tied it to a stack of books. The entire assembly is in a cardboard box to allow us to slide it back and forth. (We had to try several iterations before finding a setup that gave reasonably consistent results.)

We pulled the bus back $$33 \;\mathrm{in}$$ (inches), then allowed it to roll forward until it no longer pressed against the scale. We recorded the scale reading after $$11\;\mathrm{in}.$$ (The readings are in multiples of $$11\;\mathrm{in}$$ because we used $$11\;\mathrm{in}$$ sheets of notebook paper as a distance measurement, rather than a tape measure or meter stick.)

The scale reading was in grams, which we converted to newtons assuming $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ We also converted $${}d$$ to meters.

We repeated the measurement four times and averaged the results. A plot of $$F_{\rm push}$$ is below.

--------------

In this problem, you'll use knowledge of $$F_{\rm push}$$ to design an experiment to test Newton's second law.

We can assume that the mass of the bus doesn't affect $$F_{\rm push}.$$ This is because $$F_{\rm push}$$ is proportional to $$F_{\rm spring},$$ which should depend only on the state of the spring, not the motion of the bus or other features of the bus. (This also assumes the wheels don't slip relative to the floor.)

However, as the data in the reading problem above shows, we cannot assume that $$F_{\rm push}$$ is constant, or that it obeys Hooke's law.

We want to test the idea $$ F_{\rm net} = ma $$

We won't measure force directly in the second phase of the experiment; that is impractical when the bus is moving. Instead, we'll test whether $$ a \propto \dfrac{1}{m} $$ which is a consequence of Newton's second law.

All of the following procedures would work to test this proportionality if $$F_{\rm push}$$ were constant, but instead, let's make the following assumptions:

- $$F_{\rm push}$$ is not constant. - $$F_{\rm push}$$ depends only on $$d.$$ - The plot of $$F_{\rm push}$$ versus $${}d$$ is the same in every trial. - Newton's second law of motion is correct. - For this analysis, we ignore the error in our measurements of $$a$$ and $$m.$$

**Given these assumptions, which __one__ of the proposed procedures will give $$a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}?$$**

We are not asking whether $$a$$ described in the procedures below is the true acceleration of the bus, or whether it is truly the average acceleration of the bus over time, etc. Instead, we are asking whether the quantity we will record as $$a,$$ as described in the procedures below, will be related to mass via $$a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}.$$

**(a)** Pull the bus back $$1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in every trial. Release the bus from rest and let it run for $$2.0 \;\mathrm{s}.$$ Record $$d,$$ the distance the bus travels in $$2.0 \;\mathrm{s}.$$

The formula $$d = \dfrac12 at^2$$ is equivalent to $$a = \dfrac{2d}{t^2}$$ so plug in $${}d$$ and $$t = 2.0 \;\mathrm{s}$$ to find $$a.$$ Use the scale to find the mass $$m$$ of the bus and record that as well.

Repeat several times to get a sense of the uncertainty in the distance measurements.

Then put various items inside the bus to change its mass. Repeat the procedure, collecting new data. In each trial, we fix the time at $$t = 2.0 \;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$d$$ varies due to the changing mass. Each trial ultimately results in one value of $${}a$$ and one value of $${}m,$$ along with their uncertainties, for each mass of the bus we test.

Although the acceleration of the bus may vary over a single trial, we treat the $$a$$ value calculated in this procedure as an average acceleration over the trial, and then test whether $$a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}.$$

**(b)** Everything in this procedure is the same as in (a), with one difference. In (a), we let the bus run for a fixed time (always $$2.0 \;\mathrm{s})$$ and measured how far it traveled. Here we always let the bus travel $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ forward, and we measure the time this takes using a stopwatch. The $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ distance is chosen because this is about how far the bus can travel forward and still have $$F_{\rm push} > 0.$$

Aside from this change, do everything the same way as in (a).

**(c)**

This procedure is similar to (a) and (b), but we do not fix $${}d$$ or $${}t.$$ Every trial, we pull the bus back $$1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and release it, but we let the bus travel as far as we like and time how long it takes. We let the bus go a wide variety of distances to get more different data points.

Aside from this change, everything else is the same as procedures (a) and (b). We use different masses, we use our distance and time measurements to calculate $$a$$ for each trial with the same formula, etc.

(a)

(b)

(c)

1. Begin with the bus at a marked spot on the floor with the spring completely uncompressed. 2. It accelerates forward, pushed by friction from the floor. 4. Allow the bus to accelerate forward until it hits a rolled-up carpet. The carpet was placed $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from the point where the bus was released. Time how long it takes the bus to reach the carpet. 5. Repeat four more time (five times total) to get a sense of the spread in the data.

We conducted this entire procedure, then added some household items to the bus to increase its mass, then repeated the procedure. (We model the bus and the items inside as a single system.)

We did this for six different masses, using a kitchen scale to record the mass.

We measured distances using pieces of notebook paper laid end-to-end on the floor.

The data we collected is below $$ \begin{array}{c | c | c | c} \text{ m (g)} & \bar{t} \,\,(\mathrm{s}) & \sigma_t \,\,(\mathrm{s})\\ \hline 467 & 1.56 & 0.06 \\ 615 & 1.83 & 0.03 \\ 712 & 2.01 & 0.05 \\ 994 & 2.56 & 0.07 \\ 1261 & 3.17 & 0.05 \\ 1386 & 3.55 & 0.04 \end{array} $$

$$m$$ is the total mass of the bus plus any items inside it. The mass of the bus alone was $$467 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

$$\bar{t}$$ is the average time it took the bus to travel $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from rest.

$$\sigma_t$$ is the standard deviation of the times we collected.

The uncertainty in the mass is approximately $$1 \;\mathrm{g},$$ which is small enough to ignore.

Make a plot of this data, including error bars. You may want to attempt a best-fit line as well.

Use the plot you draw to select the best description from below.

Part D. The data in part (A) does not match the predicted shape from part (B). Also, the plot in the solution to part (C) is clearly not linear. In this question, you'll select explanations that could theoretically explain why the data don't match the theory in this experiment.

Here, we aren't judging whether the explanations are likely. Instead, we're judging whether, if they were correct, logically they would explain why our data didn't match our predictions.

For example, another explanation, not included below, is that all the distance measurements are wrong. We assumed each piece of paper was $$11 \;\mathrm{in}$$ long, some paper is $$11.7 \;\mathrm{in}$$ long. If we had the wrong type of paper, all our distance measurements would be too long by about $$6\%.$$ If that explanation were included on the list, you should not select it. The reason is that adjusting all the distance measurements would adjust all the accelerations we calculate, but it would adjust them all by the same factor. It wouldn't affect the overall shape of the graph. Therefore, while this error in the experiment is possible, it can't explain the data in part (C) not being linear.

On the other hand, another explanation could be that the distance measurements were wrong in random ways because the paper we used to make measurements slid around on the floor without us noticing. In that case, the explanation is very broad, and there exists some type of sliding of the papers at various points in the experiment that would affect our distance measurements in the right way to make the data in part (C) look like it does, instead of a straight line. This explanation isn't very likely, since we would probably have noticed the paper sliding around that much, but logically it's a conceivable explanation. If that explanation were included in the list below, it would be counted as a possible explanation.

Which one of the following could theoretically explain why the data don't match theoretical predictions in this experiment?

The question isn't asking which of (a) through (d) is likely. Instead, it's asking which, if it were true (however implausible), could potentially explain why the data and theory don't match.

**(a)** The bus is driven forward by friction on its back wheels. On the front wheels, there was a constant backward force from friction, but we neglected that. If we had included a constant backward force in our model, the theoretical prediction in part (B) would change to a good match for the data in part (A), assuming we chose the magnitude of the backward force correctly.

**(b)** We assumed $$F_{\rm push}$$ was constant, but we know it actually varied over the course of a run. We could build a new model where $$F_{\rm push}$$ varies, but the plot of $$F_{\rm push}$$ versus $$d$$ is the same for every trial. If we did that, it would change the prediction to be a good match to the data.

**(c)** The framework of Newtonian mechanics is not a good model for the acceleration of the bus.

**(d)** When the bus's mass is low, static friction with the floor is not always high enough to keep the wheels from slipping. The wheels slip a bit at low mass, relaxing the spring and lowering the force pushing the bus forward. The wheels do not slip when the bus has high mass. We don't know the exact extent of the slipping, but it means we would need to model the force as a decreasing function of the mass of the bus, rather than a constant. With this modification to the model, it would be possible to get predictions that closely match the data.

An example of slip-stick motion you may be able to reproduce at home is a __glass harp__.

Take a clean wine glass, and make sure your hands are clean as well. Wet your index finger and rub in a steady circle around the rim of a wine glass.

With some practice, you should be able to hear the glass play a note. You can pour water in the glass to change the note it plays.

To find the frequency your cup is playing, you could use a smartphone app such as PhyPhox or PhysicsToolbox. You may also have an electric tuner at home, or if you have a piano or other instrument, you could play notes on that instrument until you match the frequency of your wineglass, then look up the frequency. You could also use your computer or tablet and any digital instrument tuner webpage, either to detect the pitch using your computer's microphone, or to generate pitches of different frequencies until you match your wine glass.

**(a)** Can you find a relationship between the total mass of the cup and the frequency played? There should be a clean quantitative relationship here, and you should be able to relate it back to our understanding of harmonic oscillators. What data did you collect to answer this question, and how did you analyze the data?

**(b)** Is there a relationship between how fast you have to move your finger and the frequency? If the finger is undergoing slip-stick motion, we expect faster motion of the finger to lead to higher frequency. Our class calculation estimating the frequency of slip-stick motion in a violin is an example. (Your class may or may not have done this calculation, depending on time. If not, feel free to ask on the message boards for the relevant bit of bonus material on this topic.) Do you still get a clean quantitative relationship between finger speed and frequency, and is it the relationship you expect? Again, tell your classmates how you investigated this question and share your data.

name: Part A. We began this problem set imagining Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on another planet.
desc: Part A. We began this problem set imagining Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on another planet. Asteroids have mass, and there's gravitational acceleration near their surface. However, asteroids are small enough that the gravity there is weak, meaning Imatorbhebhe could jump very high…
statement:
Part A. We began this problem set imagining Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on another planet.

Asteroids have mass, and there's gravitational acceleration near their surface. However, asteroids are small enough that the gravity there is weak, meaning Imatorbhebhe could jump very high.

If an asteroid is small enough, Imatorbhebhe could even jump completely off it, so the asteroid's gravity would never pull him back down.

We'd like to know the size of an asteroid Imatorbhebhe could jump off, but to answer that question, we need to understand the role of __energy__ in Newton's gravitational model. That's what we'll do in this multi-part problem.

-----------------------

When objects $$A$$ and $$B$$ interact, there are gravitational forces between them.

Another perspective is that the $$AB$$ system has __gravitational potential energy__. (We'll define "the $$AB$$ system" to be the two objects, together with their gravitational interaction.)

We've already seen the the relationship between gravitational forces and gravitational potential energy in the special case of objects near the surface of Earth, where we model $$\vec{g}$$ as constant. Then we have $$\begin{aligned} \vec{F}_{g; E \to O} & = m_O \vec{g} \\ U_{g; EO} & = mgh \end{aligned}$$ where the $$O$$ subscript stands for an object and $$h$$ is the height of the object above whatever height we decide to be zero. (We might choose $$h = 0$$ at sea level, but for an experiment done in a physics classroom, we might choose $$h = 0$$ to be at the floor of the room, or the table we're working on, or even the ceiling of the room, if we want.)

Those equations only apply in the simplified model where gravitational interactions don't change with distance and always point in the same direction. This model is fine for studying everyday things like a roller coaster or an Atwood machine. To study __Celestial mechanics__ is the study of the motion of planets, stars, asteroids, galaxies, etc. we need a new model.

We want to study energy again, but this time using Newton's universal law of gravitation as a model for the force: $$ \vec{F}_{A \to B} = -\dfrac{G m_A m_B}{r_{AB}^2} \hat{r}_{A \to B}$$ (We'll assume spherical symmetry of $$A$$ and $$B,$$ which simplifies the model.)

Our goal will be to find, understand, and apply a formula for the gravitational potential energy of the $$AB$$ system. We'll call that energy $$U_{g; AB}.$$

Let's begin with dimensional analysis.

The relevant quantities are $$G, m_A, m_B,$$ and $$r_{AB}.$$

Find the proportionality between $$U_{g, AB}$$ and those quantities.

Part B. The dimensional analysis in part (A) takes us most of the way to a formula for $$U_{g;AB},$$ but to understand the meaning of this dimensional result, and to finish turning it into a complete formula, let's make an analogy with a situation where we already know equations for both force and potential energy: the ideal spring.

------------------------

Imagine a spring with one end attached to a wall. We could push on the opposite end with a force $$\vec{F}_s$$ to compress the spring.

We modeled the force required with Hooke's law, $$\vec{F}_s = k \Delta \vec{x}$$ Here, $$\Delta \vec{x}$$ is the displacement of the left hand side of the spring.

As we push the spring, its displacement and the force we exert on it are in the same direction, so we do work on the spring. That means energy enters the spring, and it stores that energy as potential energy, $$U_s = \dfrac12 k (\Delta x)^2$$

We would like to find $$U_{g; AB},$$ a potential energy formula for gravitational interactions between spheres $$A$$ and $$B.$$ The process is similar to finding the formula $$U_s$$ for springs.

We can begin by setting $$A$$ and $$B$$ on opposite ends of a flat frictionless table on Earth. The spheres will attract each other with gravitational forces.

To mimic the spring system, we will anchor sphere $$B$$ to the table. Then sphere $$A$$ will move to the right across the table, pulled by the gravitational force from $$B.$$ In real life, we wouldn't be able to measure this because the gravitational force is weak, and we can't get a table that's flat enough, frictionless enough, etc. $$A$$ moves across the table as a thought experiment.

The gravitational force from $$A$$ to $$B$$ still exists, even though we didn't draw it above. That force is cancelled by a normal force from the pin in $$B,$$ so $$B$$ doesn't move.

We could attach sphere $$A$$ to a half-Atwood machine. If the load were light enough, sphere $$A$$ could lift the load while continuing to move toward sphere $$B.$$

As sphere $$A$$ approaches sphere $$B,$$ what happens to their gravitational potential energy, $$U_{g;AB}?$$

Here, we are asking for the gravitational potential energy of the interaction __between the two spheres__, so ignore any gravitational potential energy related to interactions with the Earth.

$$U_{g; AB}$$ increases as the spheres get closer

$$U_{g; AB}$$ decreases as the spheres get closer

$$U_{g; AB}$$ stays the same as the spheres get closer

The half-Atwood machine applies a tension force $$\vec{T}$$ to sphere $$A.$$ We adjust $$\vec{T}$$ This means that, as the gravitational force $$\vec{F}_{B \to A}$$ gets continuously stronger, we continuously add mass to the load so that $$\vec{T}$$ exactly cancels $$\vec{F}_{g; B \to A}.$$ so that $$A$$ moves with some constant velocity $$\vec{v}_A.$$

Part D. Here, we use the graphs for force versus displacement from part (C) to think about work and energy in both the spring and gravitational systems.

------------

As we compress the spring, it moves to the right, and the force $$\vec{F}_s$$ we apply to it is to the right. That means the force does positive work on the spring. We can call that work $$W_{F \to s}.$$

The work done in compressing the spring a distance $$\Delta x_1$$ is the signed area between the plot of $$F_{s;x}$$ and the horizontal axis. The area begins at $$\Delta x = 0,$$ where we begin pushing. It ends at $$\Delta x_1,$$ where we finish pushing.

The work $$W_{F \to s}$$ done by the external force $$\vec{F}_s$$ on the spring is stored by the spring as potential energy $$U_s,$$ so we find $$\begin{aligned} U_s & = W_{F \to s}\\ {} & = \dfrac12 \,(\text{width of shaded region}) \cdot (\text{height of shaded region}) \\ {} & = \dfrac12 (\Delta x_1)(F_s) \\ {} & = \dfrac12 (\Delta x_1)(k \Delta x_1) \\ {} & = \dfrac12 k (\Delta x_1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Part E. At last, we're ready to return to the problem of Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping off an asteroid.

--------------------------

Having plotted $$U_{g; AB}$$ and found most of a formula for it by dimensional analysis, our knowledge is nearly equivalent to knowing the entire formula, which is below (click to reveal).

$$ U_{g; AB} = - \dfrac{Gm_A m_B}{r_{AB}}$$

Recall that we can set $$U = 0$$ wherever we want when using potential energy. The standard in physics is to set $$U_{g; AB} \to 0$$ and $$r_{AB} \to \infty.$$ In other words, spheres never have potential energy of zero, but as they get further and further apart, their potential energy gets closer and closer to zero.

The gravitational potential energy is negative, meaning that it increases (moves toward zero) as $$A$$ and $$B$$ get further apart. These features of the formula replicate your findings in parts (A) through (D).

Now we imagine Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on an asteroid. Model the asteroid as a sphere of radius $$R$$ and uniform density. Model Imatorbhebhe's jump as straight up - directly away from the center of the asteroid.

We will refer to Imatorbhebhe and the asteroid together as simply "the system."

When Imatorbhebhe is on the surface of the asteroid, he's a distance $$R$$ from its center. (We ignore Imatorbhebhe's own height.) According to the formula for $$U_g,$$ the system's potential energy is negative.

When Imatorbhebhe jumps, he gains kinetic energy. The total mechanical energy of the system becomes $$E = U_g + KE$$

(We ignore kinetic energy in the asteroid since it is far more massive than Imatorbhebhe and is negligibly pushed away when he jumps. We also work in the inertial reference frame of the asteroid.)

After Imatorbhebhe jumps, he goes higher and higher, but slows down as he rises. The system's potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases. The total mechanical energy of the system is conserved.

If the asteroid is large enough, Imatorbhebhe will eventually come back down. Otherwise, he'll continue rising forever, never turning around.

Finally, assume that the orbital period for satellites in low-Earth orbit is $$T_E = 90 \;\mathrm{min}$$ This means that a satellite orbiting just above the surface of Earth would take 90 minutes to go all the way around.

(Real satellites are a few hundred kilometers above Earth's surface, not directly at the surface, but that elevation is small compared to the radius of Earth, and we'll ignore it for this problem.)

In a previous homework set, we studied the Ikaros light sail, which can control what direction it is facing by changing its reflectivity.

As a simple model, imagine a square sheet with side length $$s$$ and mass $$m.$$ The left half of the sheet is black and absorbs all light that hits it. The right half of the sheet is reflective. All light that hits it bounces back.

Sunlight approaches the sheet directly perpendicular to the sheet.

The intensity of the sunlight is $$I_0.$$ This means that the sunlight carries power $$I_0$$ per unit area.

Recall that the momentum of light with energy $$E$$ is $$p = \dfrac{E}{c}.$$

Find a proportionality for the angular acceleration $${}\alpha$$ of the sheet about its center of mass in terms of $$I_0, m, s,$$ and $$c.$$

Also indicate whether the angular acceleration is clockwise or counterclockwise.

If you want to find the exact value of $$\alpha,$$ you'll need to know that the moment of inertia of the sheet about its center of mass is $$I = \dfrac{1}{12} ms^2.$$

Alternatively, the question doesn't require you to find the coefficient in the equation for $$\alpha,$$ so you could answer more intuitively by thinking about how each quantity should affect $$\alpha,$$ and also by thinking about the dimensions of all the quantities.

https://www.mettlesomegenius.net/blogpost/The_Bucket_Problem_04142018

Consider the bucket and water together as a system.

Let the kinetic energy of the system be $$KE_0.$$

Next, we spin the bucket twice as fast, so $$\omega_1 = 2 \omega_0.$$ We again keep the bucket spinning steadily for long enough for all the water to rotate along with the bucket. Assume that the water does not slosh out. Call the kinetic energy of the system at this point $$KE_1.$$

How does $$KE_1$$ relate to $$KE_0?$$

$$KE_1 = \dfrac14 KE_0$$

$$KE_1 = \dfrac12 KE_0$$

$$KE_1 = KE_0$$

$$KE_1 = 2 KE_0$$

$$KE_1 = 4 KE_0$$

$$KE_1 > 4 KE_0$$
