name: If a cyclist is cycling along a flat section of ground and suddenly hits a rock, their…
desc: If a cyclist is cycling along a flat section of ground and suddenly hits a rock, their bike can flip up off the ground and send the cyclist topping over the handlebars. We'll imagine that the front wheel hits the rock and stops. We'll model the rock as a point at the bottom of…
statement:
If a cyclist is cycling along a flat section of ground and suddenly hits a rock, their bike can flip up off the ground and send the cyclist topping over the handlebars.

We'll imagine that the front wheel hits the rock and stops. We'll model the rock as a point at the bottom of the front wheel, and use it as the reference point about which we calculate any torque or angular momentum.

A moment before hitting the rock, the bike was not rotating, but after hitting the rock, it starts rotating. Several students write explanations for how to account for the phenomenon in terms of torque and/or angular momentum. Choose the single best explanation.

**Azra**: The bike has linear momentum $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ before hitting the rock. When it hits the rock, the rock acts as a pivot point, converting the linear momentum into angular momentum $$L = I\omega,$$ where $${}I$$ is the moment of inertia of the bike and rider about the rock. Assuming the rider was going fast enough when they hit the rock, they will create enough angular momentum to cause them to flip all the way up and over the handlebars.

**Barrett**: When the front wheel of a bike hits a rock and is prevented from moving, the momentum of the bike and rider is still moving forward. Since the front wheel is no longer able to rotate and absorb this momentum, the force is transferred to the frame of the bike, where it becomes a torque and causes the bike to lift off the ground and rotate forward. This is due to the principle of conservation of angular momentum, which states that the total angular momentum of an isolated system remains constant unless acted upon by an external torque.

**Carina**: The wheels of a bike spin, meaning they have angular momentum. If we stop the rotation of the front wheel suddenly, all that angular momentum it had due to spinning will go into the rest of the bike. That's why the bike rotates clockwise - the front wheel was rotating clockwise as well. There doesn't need to be an external torque because the front wheel's angular momentum accounts for the rotation of the bike.

**Damini**: The bike already had angular momentum about the rock before the collision. This is because the bike had linear momentum, and its center of mass was off the ground. The height of the center of mass off the ground was the moment arm of the linear momentum. Any force from the rock on the bike creates zero torque about the rock because the moment arm of that force is zero. This means that aside from any torque from gravity or normal forces on the bike, angular momentum of the bike is conserved after hitting the rock. The angular momentum of the bike and rider as they start rotating around the rock is approximately the same as the angular momentum they had before the collision.

Barrett

Carina

Damini

Part A. Imagine that every human on Earth gathered on the equator.

Everyone syncs up their watches, and at a prescribed moment, everyone starts moving in the opposite direction as Earth's rotation (i.e. west) at $$1.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Which best describes what would happen to Earth when the people start moving, and as they continue moving around the equator?

Consider Earth to be a separate system than all the people on it. Model Earth as a uniform, solid sphere. Ignore the force from the Sun and any other outside influences.

For this problem, we're interested in what the effect would be, even if that effect is likely too small to measure.

No effect at all on Earth.

Earth would experience constant acceleration.

Earth would experience constant angular acceleration that increases its angular speed.

Earth would experience constant angular acceleration that decreases its angular speed.

Earth's angular speed would quickly undergo a small increase as people accelerated, then remain constant as long as everyone kept moving.

Earth's angular speed would quickly undergo a small decrease as people accelerated, then remain constant as long as everyone kept moving.

desc: Part A. In 1967, scientists turned on the Interplanetary Scintillation Array, a radio telescope spanning about four acres of land…
statement:
Part A. In 1967, scientists turned on the Interplanetary Scintillation Array, a radio telescope spanning about four acres of land.

https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co8105496/parts-from-the-cambridge-interplanetary-scintillation-array-radio-telescope-instrument-component

The telescope picked up a signal that the lead astronomer Antony Hewish believed was simply noise. Graduate student Jocelyn Bell was working on the project under Hewish's supervision, and believed the data could be important. Bell and Hewish took new data and found that the signal was pulsing every $$1.337 \;\mathrm{s}.$$ Bell then discovered another pulsing radio source with a different frequency.

Astronomers at the time didn't know of any natural phenomenon that could produce extremely regular pulsing, and Bell and Hewish nicknamed the signals "LGM" for "little green men," a joke that the signal must be generated by aliens.

The radio sources eventually became known as __pulsars__. Hewish was awarded a Nobel Prize for the discovery, but the Nobel comittee neglected to include Bell in the prize.

Today, pulsars are known to be __neutron stars__ - giant balls of neutrons jammed up next to each other. (Matter is made mostly of protons, neutrons, and electrons, but in neutron stars the protons and electrons combine and turn into neutrons.) Neutron stars aren't burning balls of plasma. Instead, they're the remnants of __former__ burning balls of plasma.

Neutron stars are formed from stars called __supergiants__. When supergiants burn through all their fuel, they collapse under their own gravity, forming neutron stars, some of which appear to us as pulsars.

Pulsars emit radiation continuously, but only in the directions of their magnetic poles. They appear to pulse because they are spinning rapidly.

By Michael Kramer - http://www.jb.man.ac.uk/~mkramer/Animations.html, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2848650

The supergiant stars pulsars are formed from don't spin nearly this rapidly. They spin faster and faster as they collapse. The effect is similar to that seen in the toy "Hoberman sphere":

https://imgur.com/gallery/7h5GvdK

Model a supergiant star as a solid sphere of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R_0.$$ During the collapse of the supergiant into a pulsar, assume that the mass is conserved, but the radius decreases to $$R_f.$$ The process is isolated from outside influences.

Model the supergiant star as rotating with period $$T_0.$$ Let rotation period of the pulsar it collapses into be $$T_f.$$

If the density of the supergiant star is $$\rho_0,$$ what is the density of the pulsar in terms of $$\dfrac{T_f}{T_0}?$$

mathjax: $$ \rho_f = \rho_0 \left(\dfrac{T_f}{T_0}\right)^\blank$$

allowed: -1.023456789/

Part B. The red supergiant Betelgeuse is likely to collapse into a neutron star.

Some approximate data on Betelgeuse is

$$\begin{aligned} T_0 & \approx 40 \;\mathrm{y} \\ R_0 & \approx 5 \times 10^{11} \;\mathrm{m} \\ M & \approx 4 \times 10^{31} \;\mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}$$

When stars collapse into neutron stars, the neutron stars all have about the same density - the density of neutrons shoved up next to each other with no space in between. (In ordinary materials, the neutrons and protons are at the nucleus of each atom, and are far apart from each other compared to the size of the nucleus.) This density is $$ \rho_f \approx 4 \times 10^{17} \;\mathrm{kg/m^3} $$

Under the model of formation of neutron stars used in part (A), what will the rotational period of Betelgeuse be when it collapses?

Give your answer in normalized scientific notation. Give only one significant figure.

mathjax: $$ T_f \approx \blank \times 10^{\blank} \;\mathrm{s} $$

Part C. There is a significant discrepancy between the value you calculated in part (B) and the observed rates of pulsars. The fastest known pulsars have periods of around $$10^{-3} \;\mathrm{s},$$ and you should have found a period significantly less than that for the expected period of Betelgeuse after it collapses.

Which **two** of the following could account or partially account for this discrepancy, if it were correct?

Note that you are not judging whether these explanations are accurate. You're only judging whether, if what they say is true, they account for the real rotation period of pulsars being longer than the calculation in part (B).

Our mass and radius measurements of Betelgeuse were okay, but its density decreases considerably with distance from its center, unlike our model.

Our density estimate for the neutron star was okay for an average density, but the density of a neutron star decreases considerably with distance from the center.

We assumed the mass was constant during the collapse, but supergiants shed most of their mass in a supernove explosion before collapsing. The mass shed in the supernove can carry angular momentum away as well.

The rotation rate we used for Betelgeuse was for the surface, but the core of the star is rotating with an angular frequency considerably higher.

desc: Earlier in this problem set, we estimated how the Earth's angular speed would change if people started moving in the same direction around the equator. The effect was minuscule. Earth's rotational period does change, though. For example, earthquakes can move the mass of Earth…
statement:
Earlier in this problem set, we estimated how the Earth's angular speed would change if people started moving in the same direction around the equator. The effect was minuscule.

Earth's rotational period does change, though. For example, earthquakes can move the mass of Earth around, changing the moment of inertia and thereby changing the rotational period. The length of a day changes by up to a few microseconds after some large earthquakes.

Seasonal processes, such as changes to the jet streams, also move mass around on Earth, affecting the moment of inertia and length of the day.

Over billions of years, the largest influence on the rotational period of Earth comes from the Moon.

The Moon is responsible for tides. Tides slosh water back and forth, and this dissipates kinetic energy. As it loses kinetic energy, Earth's angular velocity decreases.

**Over time, does the tidal interaction between the Earth and the Moon push the Moon further away from Earth, pull the Moon in closer to Earth, or neither?**

Explain your reasoning. Be quantitative. Your reasoning can include: - the idea that tides dissipate mechanical energy, and Earth's angular velocity is decreasing. - ideas about angular momentum. - ideas about orbits, such as Kepler's third law.

You can assume that the Moon's orbit is circular, and that it is "tidally locked," meaning that the same side of it always faces Earth. You can also ignore the center-of-mass motion of the Earth. You can also ignore any outside influences on the Earth-Moon system, such as gravitational forces from the Sun or other planets. Finally, you can assume that the moment of inertia of Earth is constant.

It may be helpful to find the angular momentum of the Moon's orbit as a function of $$r,$$ the Earth-Moon distance. It might also be helpful to focus on proportionalities, rather than complete equations. You should not need to look up the mass of the Moon, the radius of Earth, etc. Those values aren't necessary to answer this question.

statement:
Part A. Kǒngmíng lanterns, or __sky lanterns__, are lanterns with a candle inside that can rise up into the air, like a hot air balloon.

(Sky lanterns are illegal in many areas because they can cause fires. Please don't build one unless you are at an event with approval from local fire safety officials.)

These lanterns were invented in China, perhaps by Zhuge Liang some time in the early third century CE. (Some historians believe they date back hundreds of years earlier.) Today, they are used in festivals, but in ancient China they were also used for military signaling.

In this problem, we'll imagine designing a sky lantern. One of the first steps to this design process would be estimating how light the sky lantern needs to be, given its size. That puts constraints on how much material and what type of material can go into the design.

Part D. To estimate the mass of materials we should use in a sky lantern, we need to know how the density of hot air is different than that of cold air.

Air can be modeled closely by an equation called __Charles's law__ after French scientist Jacques Charles. It is an empirical law based on experimental data.

We can state the law as $$\rho \propto \dfrac{1}{T}$$ where $$\rho$$ is the density of air and $$T$$ is the temperature.

However, to use this law, we must measure $$T$$ using an __absolute__ temperature scale, such as the Kelvin scale. In this scale, temperature is measured in units called __kelvin__, $$\mathrm{K}.$$

A change in temperature of $$1 \;\mathrm{K}$$ is equivalent to a change of temperature of $$1 \;\mathrm{C}.$$ However, Kelvin temperatures are 273.15 degrees higher than Celsius temperatures.

For example, if the temperature in a room rises from $$20^\circ \;\mathrm{C}$$ to $$23^\circ \;\mathrm{C},$$ then in the Kelvin scale we'd say the temperature rises from $$293.15 \;\mathrm{K}$$ to $$296.15 \;\mathrm{K}.$$

Suppose we want to build a sky lantern with a radius $$r = 30 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ and a height $$h = 90 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$ From tests with a candle, we find that the candle can heat the air from $$10^\circ \;\mathrm{C}$$ to $$50^\circ \;\mathrm{C},$$ and we expect the outdoor temperature to be about $$10^\circ \;\mathrm{C}$$ at the launch event. The density of our atmosphere at this temperature is approximately $$(1.2 \times 10^{-3} )\;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$.

What is the maximum mass $$m_{\rm max}$$ we can use for the materials that go into building the sky lantern, including the candle (but not the air inside it)?

statement:
This is the final writing problem in the course. It's a short lab writeup. Although this problem is about Archimedes's principle, the goal is to give you practice __designing__ experiments, not to confirm a specific physics model.

--------------

Archimedes's principle says that if a floating boat of mass $$m$$ has a displacement $$V_d$$ of water then $$ \rho_w V_d = m$$ with $$\rho_w$$ the density of the water.

By now, we've had a number of lab assignments in this course, and you've worked on questions on designing and interpreting experiments in homework and in class.

For this week, design your own experiment to test Archimedes's principle quantitatively.

You should be able to make measurements with relative uncertainty of $$10\%$$ or less, but you don't need to explicitly quantify your uncertainty. Just briefly explain how you minimized uncertainty and what effect it has on your results.

Submit: - A brief description of your setup - What you measured and what your measurements showed - A brief analysis of how well your measurements agreed with Archimedes's principle

Your writeup should take no more than one side of one page, plus potentially one more for figures / graphs.

Feel free to include pictures or diagrams to help describe your experiment. You do not need to include background on the experiment or a quantitative analysis of error. A good format would be to include three sections:

**Methods**

This section describes how you set up your experiment and what measurements you took.

**Results**

This section reports the results of your measurements. A table or graph could be sufficient as long as it is easy to interpret given what you wrote in the methods section.

**Conclusion**

This section discusses the meaning of your results and how well they agree with Archimedes's principle.

Part A. Physicists have been interested in the circulatory system for a few reasons. One is for medical applications - measurements of the speed and volume of blood flow through the circulatory system are important data for doctors treating or diagnosing issues such as cardiovascular diseases, heart valve problems, and thrombosis.

Scientists have also built models of the circulatory system to try to understand the differences between animals of different sizes. For example, physicist Geoffrey West collaborated with biologists James Brown and Brian Enquist to build a model to explain surprising facts, such as that as mammals get larger, their heart rates slow down and their lifetimes get longer, so that (roughly speaking) mammals of all sizes have about the same number of heartbeats in their lives.

In this problem we will get a very brief introduction to the application of fluid dynamics to the circulatory system.

----------------------------

Blood is carried out from the heart via the aorta, the largest of the arteries. The aorta branches many times into smaller arteries. The smaller arteries eventually lead into veins, which return the blood to the heart.

By OpenStax College - Anatomy & Physiology, Connexions Web site. http://cnx.org/content/col11496/1.6/, Jun 19, 2013., CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=30148241

Suppose an artery has radius $$r$$ and blood moves through it at speed $$v.$$

The artery branches into two arteries, each of radius $$r/2.$$

The speed of blood is $$v_2$$ in each of the two smaller arteries. Assume the blood moves parallel to the artery wall and has the same speed all across the artery cross section in each case.

What is $$v_2?$$

Part B. To transition from arteries to veins, blood flows through __capillaries__.

By Community Emergency Response Team - http://www.citizencorps.gov/cert/IS317/medops/medops/ic_04_02_0091.htm, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=29582984

Capillaries are very narrow so that oxygen can diffuse from them into the body. There are capillaries all over your body, delivering oxygen to your cells. You can assume that all the blood that leaves the aorta eventually goes through one capillary before returning to the heart.

Some data on the circulatory system is $$\begin{aligned} v_a & = 100 \;\mathrm{cm/s} \\ r_a & = 1.2 \;\mathrm{cm} \\ v_c & = 0.1 \;\mathrm{cm/s} \\ r_c & = 5 \times 10^{-4} \;\mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}$$ where the $$a$$ subscript stands for the aorta and the $$c$$ subscript stands for a typical capillary.

Given this data, how many capillaries are there in a human body?

Give your answer to one significant figure.

mathjax: $$ N \approx \blank \times 10^{\blank}$$

width: 1,2

allowed: 1023456789

Part C. Bernoulli's equation fails miserably to describe the circulatory system. That equation assumes conservation of mechanical energy, meaning it assumes there is no friction. On the scale of capillaries, flow is dominated by friction.

In high-friction situations like a capillary, a better model for the flow uses the Hagen–Poiseuille equation,

$$ \Delta P = \dfrac{8 \mu L v}{r^2} $$ where $$\Delta P$$ is the pressure change from one side of a blood vessel to another.

$$\mu$$ is a property of fluids called the __viscosity__. You can assume it is constant.

$${L}$$ is the length of the blood vessel. $$v$$ is the speed of blood through the blood vessel. $$r$$ is the radius of the blood vessel.

For example, in a capillary, $$\Delta P$$ would be the pressure at the artery side of the capillary minus the pressure at the vein side of the capillary. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation would let us calculate $$\Delta P$$ reasonably well.

Imagine doubling the radii of all capillaries in the body while keeping the __total volume__ of blood flowing through them per unit time the same. The number of capillaries is also kept the same.

If the initial pressure across each capillary was $$\Delta P_0,$$ what would the pressure difference $$\Delta P_2$$ be after doubling the capillary radii?

Give your answer as a decimal.

mathjax: $$ \Delta P_2 = \blank\Delta P_0 $$

statement:
A scientist has a closed tank of water. A floating ball $$F$$ sits on the surface of the water, and a sinking ball $${}S$$ sits at the bottom of the tank.

The tank is equipped with a board that shakes up and down to make waves. The scientist sets the board oscillating, making waves that travel from left to right along the tank.

There is a common model that explains how waves move in deep water. This model predicts that $${}F$$ will go in circles as the waves pass by, but will not drift in any particular direction over the long term, so that its average velocity over a long time is zero. Below is an animation of this model.

Alexander C, "Waves on the surface of water HD", YouTube

The tank is not In physics, we always compare the size of a system to some other size when saying how big the system is. For water to be "deep," there is no fixed depth, such as $$1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ or $$10 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Instead, the water needs to be deep compared to the wavelength of the waves. For example, if the wave peaks are $$20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ apart, the tank would be "deep" if it were more than about $$2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ deep, since $$2 \;\mathrm{m} \gg 20 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$, though, and $${}F$$ drifts gradually to the right in addition to moving in circles.

Below is the scientist's data, with the path of $${}F$$ tracked by some computer vision software.

Justin Pringle, Twitter

**What is the most likely motion of $${}S$$ while $${}F$$ is drifting to the right?**

You can assume that the balls get pushed along with the water, so their motion is the same as the motion of the water they are next to, i.e., the balls are a convenient way of visualizing the motion of the water.

You can also assume that the average drift velocity in the $${}x$$ direction, as a function of height above the bottom of the tank, either increases, decreases, or remains steady as the height increases, but doesn't do a combination of those, i.e., that function is monotonic.

Use continuity and volume conservation to help you. If water is drifting to the right along the top of the tank, what must it be doing along the bottom?

drifting to the right at about the same speed as $$F$$

drifting to the right, but slower than $$F$$

drifting to the right, but faster than $$F$$

More than half the cylinder is underwater when it floats.

The cylinder floats at some equilibrium position based on its density relative to water.

We could apply a vertical force $$F_y$$ to the cylinder, displacing it an amount $$y$$ from equilibrium.

Define the signs so that when we push down, $$F_y < 0$$ and $$y<0.$$ When we lift up, $$F_y > 0$$ and $$y > 0.$$

**Which one of the following is a plot of $$y$$ versus $$F_y?$$**

Assume the container of water is very wide compared to the cylinder, so the surface of the water doesn't move up or down appreciably.

Because more than half the cylinder is underwater when floating freely, we know $$\rho_w > \rho > \dfrac12 \rho_w.$$

The plot was drawn with $$\rho = 0.75 \rho_w,$$ but you don't need to know this exact value. You do need to know $$\rho > \rho_w/2.$$

Then $$y,$$ the displacement of the cylinder from equilibrium, would oscillate in time.

As a simple model, we could assume that the net force on the cylinder as a function of $$y$$ is equal to $$F_y,$$ the force we identified in part (A).

Under this assumption, what would the oscillation period of the cylinder be?

Part C. As the cylinder in part (B) oscillates, its displacement changes. If the cylinder moves down, it needs to push water out of the way. When the cylinder moves up, water needs to come in to fill the space that would otherwise be left behind.

**If we include this motion of the water in our model, what would happen to the oscillation period of the cylinder?**

You can continue to assume that the surface of the water stays flat, for example ignoring any waves the cylinder generates.

Try thinking about this in terms of energy. We can find the frequency of a harmonic oscillator by thinking about the potential energy and kinetic energy involved. When we add in the motion of the water, we don't change the potential energy stored in the cylinder-water system, but we do increase the kinetic energy the system has for a given motion of the cylinder.

statement:
Part A. A water bottle has an open top. There is water in the bottle to height $$h$$ above the bottom of the bottle. You poke a hole in the side of the bottle at height $$y.$$ Water comes streaming horizontally out of the hole and follows a parabola to the ground. It hits the ground a distance $${}d$$ from the bottom of the water bottle.

Several students are discussing the problem of how to choose $$y$$ to maximize $$d.$$

**Select the one student whose claim is incorrect, given the models we've studied in this class.**

**Garnet** says: "We can use conservation of energy to find the speed $$v$$ of the water as it leaves the hole."

**Amethyst** says: "Or we can use Bernoulli's equation. It gives the same result."

**Pearl** says: "Or we can use $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$ to find that speed. The interpretations are: $$\begin{aligned} A_1 &: \text{ surface area of water at the top surface inside the bottle} \\ v_1 &: \text{ speed that the top surface moves downward} \\ A_2 &: \text{ area of hole}\\ v_2 &: \text{ speed of water as it leaves the hole} \end{aligned}$$ This equation would also let us find $$v_2$$ without using Bernoulli's equation or conservation of energy."

**Steven** says: "We can use kinematic equations like $$y = \dfrac12 g t^2$$ to model the motion of the water after it leaves the bottle. Here, $${}t$$ would be the time it takes any little bit of water to hit the ground after leaving the hole."

**Peridot** says: "The size of the hole won't affect $$d,$$ assuming $$d \ll y,$$ since making the hole a little larger doesn't change how fast the water comes out."
